question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
Analia ends up controlling both. Analia's Lay Claim enchants Nico's Corrupted Conscience and says "You control enchanted permanent," so Analia gains control of Corrupted Conscience. Corrupted Conscience in turn says "You control enchanted creature" — "you" means Corrupted Conscience's controller, which is now Analia — so Analia also gains control of Bane Alley Blackguard (which she also owns).

Why: an Aura's controller is tracked separately from the controller of what it enchants [303.4e], and control-changing effects are all applied together in layer 2 [613.1b]. When layer 2 is applied, Lay Claim first makes Analia the controller of Corrupted Conscience; Corrupted Conscience's own control effect then depends on that result, so it grants Bane Alley Blackguard to Analia rather than to Nico. Nico controls nothing here afterward.

Note the flip side of the general principle in [Lay Claim ruling #0]: gaining control of a permanent doesn't hand you the Auras attached to it, and an Aura's "you" refers to that Aura's own controller. Here that works in Analia's favor because Lay Claim targeted the Aura itself, not the creature.

This analysis is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; no other player is involved. (If Nico were later to leave a multiplayer game, that wouldn't matter — neither Lay Claim nor Corrupted Conscience would be owned or controlled by Nico at that point.)

However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — Iroas, God of Victory is a creature, and it's 4/4.

Assumptions: Alan's devotion to red and white is less than seven (they say devotion to white is 2, and nothing indicates seven or more red/white symbols), so Iroas, God of Victory's own ability is active; and with Starfield of Nyx resolved Alan controls five enchantments (Iroas, God of Victory + 3 others + Starfield of Nyx). Iroas, God of Victory is not an Aura, so Starfield of Nyx's ability applies to it.

Why:
- Devotion is counted first: per CR 700.5a, devotion is calculated after copy/control/text-changing effects but before other characteristic-modifying effects, so Iroas, God of Victory's {R} and {W} do count, and with devotion to red and white under seven its own ability tries to make it not a creature.
- Both Iroas, God of Victory's "isn't a creature" ability and Starfield of Nyx's "is a creature in addition to its other types" are type-changing effects applied in layer 4 (CR 613.1, 613.1g), and within a layer they apply in timestamp order (CR 613.4a references timestamp order; CR 613.6 shows layered parts of one effect). Neither is dependent on the other. Starfield of Nyx entered later, so its timestamp is later and it applies last: Iroas, God of Victory ends up a Legendary Enchantment Creature — God.
- Starfield of Nyx also sets base power and toughness equal to mana value. That part applies in layer 7b to the same object (CR 613.6, and see CR 613.5 / 302.4c for how P/T is built up). Iroas, God of Victory's mana cost is {2}{R}{W}, mana value 4, so its base P/T becomes 4/4, overriding the printed 7/4. With no counters or other pumps, it's 4/4.

If instead Alan's devotion to red and white were seven or more, Iroas, God of Victory would be a creature from its own ability too — but it would still be 4/4, because Starfield of Nyx's base-setting effect applies regardless.

Player count doesn't matter here: devotion counts only permanents Alan controls, and none of the rules involved differ between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

question: Alex activates [Inkmoth Nexus] to turn it into a creature and attacks Nadia with it. Nadia doesn't block it and then casts [Summoning Trap], putting [Melira, Sylvok Outcast] onto the battlefield. What happens during the combat damage step?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus deals 1 normal combat damage to Nadia, and she loses 1 life — no poison counter.

Why: Melira, Sylvok Outcast says "Creatures your opponents control lose infect." Inkmoth Nexus is a creature Alex controls (a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature with flying and infect until end of turn), so once Melira, Sylvok Outcast is on the battlefield, Inkmoth Nexus loses infect [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #3]. Infect is the ability that makes damage to players become poison counters and damage to creatures become -1/-1 counters instead [702.90b, 702.90c]; with it gone, Inkmoth Nexus's combat damage is ordinary damage, so Nadia loses 1 life.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Summoning Trap resolved and put Melira, Sylvok Outcast onto the battlefield before the combat damage step began (e.g., during the declare blockers step). That's the only way it can matter here — once the combat damage step begins, damage is assigned and then dealt as turn-based actions with no priority in between [703.4k, 703.4m, 510.1, 510.2], so nothing can be cast after assignment to change the outcome. If Melira, Sylvok Outcast somehow arrived only after combat damage was dealt, Inkmoth Nexus would still have had infect and Nadia would have gotten 1 poison counter instead.

Belt and suspenders: even if Inkmoth Nexus somehow kept infect (say a later-timestamped effect regranted it), Melira, Sylvok Outcast's "You can't get poison counters" would stop the poison counter, and Nadia would neither lose life nor get a counter, though damage would still be considered dealt for abilities that care [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players. Melira, Sylvok Outcast strips infect from creatures controlled by all of Nadia's opponents, and Nadia only takes damage from creatures attacking her.

question: Nathaniel controls a [Melira, Sylvok Outcast]. Ari activates [Inkmoth Nexus] to turn it into a creature and attacks Nathaniel with it. Nathaniel doesn't block. What happens during the combat damage step?
answer:
Nothing actually happens to Nathaniel: Inkmoth Nexus deals 1 combat damage to him, but he neither loses life nor gets a poison counter.

Why:

1. Inkmoth Nexus's activated ability animates it as a 1/1 creature with flying and infect. Melira, Sylvok Outcast says "Creatures your opponents control lose infect," but Melira, Sylvok Outcast was already on the battlefield when Ari activated Inkmoth Nexus, so the ability-granting effect from Inkmoth Nexus has the later timestamp and wins. Inkmoth Nexus therefore has infect in this combat. This is exactly the situation described in [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1] (an opponent's creature gaining infect after Melira, Sylvok Outcast is out; timestamp order decides).

2. In the combat damage step, unblocked Inkmoth Nexus assigns its combat damage to the player it's attacking, Nathaniel [510.1b], and that damage is dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action with no priority in between [510.2] [703.4m] [120.2a].

3. Damage is then processed into its results [120.4b] [120.4c]. Because Inkmoth Nexus has infect, the damage does not cause Nathaniel to lose life [702.90b] [120.3b] — instead it would give him 1 poison counter. But Melira, Sylvok Outcast's other ability, "You can't get poison counters," stops that. So no life loss and no poison counter: the damage has no result at all.

4. Note that the damage was still dealt. Anything that merely checks whether damage was dealt (lifelink, "whenever this deals combat damage to a player" triggers, etc.) would still see it [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1] [120.4b].

Timing note: this assumes Melira, Sylvok Outcast was already on the battlefield before Inkmoth Nexus was animated, as stated. If Melira, Sylvok Outcast entered after the animation, Melira, Sylvok Outcast's effect would have the later timestamp and Inkmoth Nexus would lose infect [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #3]; then the 1 damage would simply cause Nathaniel to lose 1 life [120.3a].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players — Melira, Sylvok Outcast's abilities protect only Nathaniel, so an infect attacker aimed at a different opponent would still deal poison counters to that player normally. (Melira, Sylvok Outcast's "creatures your opponents control lose infect" would still apply from Nathaniel's perspective, but the timestamp analysis above is unchanged.)

question: Autumn controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue" and [Sword of Body and Mind]. Nico casts [Gift of Tusks] targeting the Painter's Servant. After it resolves, what happens if Autumn tries to equip Painter's Servant with Sword of Body and Mind?
answer:
The equip works, and Sword of Body and Mind stays attached.

Why: Gift of Tusks makes Painter's Servant lose all abilities and become a green Elephant with base power and toughness 3/3. Losing all abilities removes Painter's Servant's color-changing ability, so nothing is making other objects blue anymore [113.10]. (Even while that ability worked, Gift of Tusks' own color-setting effect would apply on top of it for Painter's Servant itself [Painter's Servant ruling #4].)

Equip {2} means "{2}: Attach this permanent to target creature you control. Activate only as a sorcery" [702.6a]. Painter's Servant is still a creature Autumn controls, so it's a legal target, and Sword of Body and Mind can legally be attached to a creature [301.5c]. The {2} is two generic mana, payable with any color or with colorless mana.

On resolution, Sword of Body and Mind attaches (receiving a new timestamp) [701.3c] and grants +2/+2 and protection from green and from blue. Protection would make an Equipment fall off as a state-based action only if that Equipment itself has the stated quality [702.16d, 704.1]. Sword of Body and Mind is a colorless artifact — it is neither green nor blue, because Painter's Servant's ability is gone. So it stays on, and Painter's Servant is a 5/5 green Elephant with protection from green and from blue until end of turn.

Contrast: if Painter's Servant still had its ability naming blue, Sword of Body and Mind would be blue and would immediately become unattached as a state-based action while remaining on the battlefield [702.16d].

Timing note: this assumes Autumn activates equip after Gift of Tusks has fully resolved, as stated. If Autumn had already attached Sword of Body and Mind before Gift of Tusks resolved, the Sword would have been blue (from Painter's Servant) and would have fallen off as soon as protection from blue applied; after Gift of Tusks resolves it could then be re-equipped as described.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same with two players or more.

question: Nathanael controls [Grizzly Bears] and [Muraganda Petroglyphs]. They cast and resolve [Crowd's Favor], targeting Grizzly Bears. Amia then casts [Archetype of Courage]. After it resolves, what are the power and toughness of Grizzly Bears?
answer:
Grizzly Bears ends up 5/4.

Why: the layer system (CR 613.1) is applied continuously and automatically, and all its results are instantaneous (CR 613.5), so you re-evaluate after Archetype of Courage resolves.

- Layer 6 (abilities): Crowd's Favor granted Grizzly Bears first strike. Archetype of Courage, controlled by Amia (Nathanael's opponent), has a later timestamp and says creatures your opponents control lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike (CR 613.7). So Grizzly Bears loses first strike and now has no abilities at all.
- Layer 7c (modifications, CR 613.4c): Muraganda Petroglyphs checks the state after layer 6. Grizzly Bears now has no abilities, so it gets +2/+2 — 4/4. Note that a granted ability is a real ability for this check, while a mere quality or characteristic-setting effect is not (CR 113.12); once the granted first strike is stripped, Grizzly Bears qualifies again.
- Also in layer 7c: Crowd's Favor's +1/+0 keeps applying — its power/toughness effect doesn't go away just because the granted ability was removed. Base 2/2 → +2/+2 → +1/+0 = 5/4.

So Grizzly Bears is a 5/4 with no first strike (and it can't gain first strike while Archetype of Courage is on the battlefield).

Timing assumption: Crowd's Favor fully resolved before Archetype of Courage was cast, as stated. Had Archetype of Courage been on the battlefield first, Grizzly Bears would never have gained first strike at all, and the result would be the same 5/4.

Player count: this works identically in a two-player game or a multiplayer game — Archetype of Courage affects creatures controlled by each of its controller's opponents, so any number of opponents' creatures are stripped of first strike the same way.

question: Albert controls [Life and Limb], [Blood Moon], and [Murmuring Bosk], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Murmuring Bosk a creature?
answer:
No. Murmuring Bosk is not a creature — it's just a nonbasic land with the land subtype Mountain (and its "{T}: Add {W} or {B}. This land deals 1 damage to you." ability, plus the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}" from being a Mountain).

Why: both Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Life and Limb ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") are continuous effects that change types/subtypes, so they both apply in layer 4 (types), with Life and Limb also touching color (layer 5) and power/toughness (layer 7b). Timestamps alone would put Life and Limb first, but dependency governs: applying Blood Moon changes what Life and Limb applies to (it strips the Forest subtype from Murmuring Bosk), the two are in the same layer, and neither is a characteristic-defining ability. So Blood Moon applies first.

After Blood Moon, Murmuring Bosk's land subtype is Mountain only — Murmuring Bosk is no longer a Forest, so Life and Limb never applies to it at all, in any layer. It gets no creature type, no green color, and no 1/1 power/toughness. Note Murmuring Bosk is nonbasic (it has the Forest land type but not the "basic" supertype), which is exactly why Blood Moon catches it [305.8, 205.4c, Murmuring Bosk ruling #0].

Collateral points: since Murmuring Bosk isn't a creature, it can't attack or block [506.3f]. If instead Blood Moon left the battlefield, Murmuring Bosk would immediately be a Forest again and Life and Limb would make it a 1/1 green Saproling creature Forest land, subject to summoning sickness [Life and Limb ruling #0]. Also, a basic Forest Albert controls would still be a 1/1 Saproling creature, because Blood Moon doesn't touch basic lands. None of this depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Angelica controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Sheltered Thicket], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Sheltered Thicket a creature?
answer:
No. Angelica's Sheltered Thicket is not a creature; it's just a land with the land type Mountain (and it retains its own text, including "This land enters tapped" and cycling).

Why: both Blood Moon and Life and Limb are type-changing continuous effects applied in layer 4 of CR 613. Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," which sets the land types of every nonbasic land to just Mountain — so Sheltered Thicket's printed Mountain Forest subtype line becomes only Mountain, and it is no longer a Forest. Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types," so it only applies to permanents that are Forests (or Saprolings). Since Blood Moon has stripped the Forest type from Sheltered Thicket, Life and Limb never applies to it at all — not in layer 4 (types), not in layer 5 (green), and not in layer 7b (1/1). Sheltered Thicket is a noncreature permanent and therefore has no power or toughness (CR 208.3a).

Ordering note: the timestamps here don't change the result. Blood Moon entered first, so it applies first anyway; and even if Life and Limb had the earlier timestamp, applying Blood Moon would change what Life and Limb applies to, making Life and Limb dependent on Blood Moon under CR 613.8a and pushing it later regardless. Also per CR 205.3c/Life and Limb ruling #3, Forest is a land type, not a creature type, which is exactly the type Blood Moon overwrites.

Contrast: a basic Forest Angelica controls would be unaffected by Blood Moon (it only hits nonbasic lands) and so would still be a 1/1 green Saproling creature Forest land under Life and Limb, with summoning sickness applying (Life and Limb ruling #0).

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Alfred controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
Alfred's Saproling token is a 1/1 green Saproling Mountain creature land — it's a creature and a land, and it taps for {R} rather than {G}.

How it gets there:

1. The token was created as a 1/1 green Saproling creature token with no other characteristics ([111.3]).
2. Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." So the Saproling token gains the land card type and the Forest land subtype while keeping creature/Saproling ([Life and Limb ruling #3], which confirms each such permanent has card types creature and land and subtypes Forest and Saproling, with Forest staying a land subtype and Saproling staying a creature type).
3. Because Life and Limb makes the Saproling token a land, and the token has no "basic" supertype, it is a nonbasic land ([Nonbasic Land], [205.4b] — nothing here grants it the basic supertype).
4. Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." That applies to the Saproling token now that it is a nonbasic land, setting its land subtype to Mountain and removing the Forest subtype. Blood Moon's effect can only be evaluated after Life and Limb's, since Life and Limb is what puts the token into the set of nonbasic lands; both are type-changing effects that apply in layer 4 ([613.6]).
5. As a Mountain, it has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" and no longer has "{T}: Add {G}" ([305.6], [Mountain], [Forest]).
6. Life and Limb still sets its power and toughness to 1/1 in layer 7b, and it remains green — once an effect starts applying to an object it keeps applying to it in the other layers even though the object is no longer a Forest ([613.6]).

So: a 1/1 green Saproling Mountain creature land that taps for {R}. Note it is still summoning-sick as a creature unless it has been under Alfred's control since his most recent turn began.

Caveat on ordering: I've applied Life and Limb before Blood Moon because Blood Moon's set of affected objects depends on Life and Limb's result. The provided context includes the layer rule ([613.6]) but not the full dependency rule text, so that step rests on the layer-4 reasoning above rather than a quoted dependency rule.

This answer doesn't change with player count — both Blood Moon and Life and Limb affect all such permanents regardless of controller, so the result is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Alex controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
Alex's Saproling token is a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a nonbasic land with the land type Mountain, and it has "{T}: Add {R}" instead of "{T}: Add {G}."

Step by step:

1. Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." The token is a Saproling, so Life and Limb makes it a creature land: card types creature and land, subtypes Saproling and Forest, with Forest correlating to the land type and Saproling to the creature type [Life and Limb ruling #3]. As a land it enters/exists as a land permanent, and land-enters triggers see it [Life and Limb ruling #1].

2. Tokens created this way have only the characteristics the creating effect gave them, so it has no "basic" supertype [111.3]. A land without the basic supertype is a nonbasic land [Basic] [Nonbasic Land] [205.4b].

3. Because it is a nonbasic land, Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" applies. It loses its other land types (Forest) and their abilities, gains the land type Mountain, and gains "{T}: Add {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #2] [305.6]. Blood Moon entered after Life and Limb, so its later effect governs which basic land type sticks; Life and Limb keeps applying to it as a Saproling, but the Forest type it grants is overwritten by Mountain.

4. Losing the Forest land type doesn't stop Life and Limb from applying, because the token is still a Saproling — so it remains a 1/1 green Saproling creature, and it's affected by summoning sickness (it can't attack or use {T} abilities, including the mana ability, until it has been under Alex's control since their most recent turn began).

Note the token is still a Saproling creature and a land at the same time; changing its subtypes doesn't add or remove supertypes [205.4b], so it never becomes basic. This answer doesn't depend on the number of players — both enchantments affect the permanents globally regardless of whether it's a two-player or multiplayer game.

One assumption: I'm reading the order given (Life and Limb, then Blood Moon, then the token) as the order the permanents entered. Even if Blood Moon had entered before Life and Limb, the token would still be a nonbasic land Saproling creature; only which basic land type/mana ability sticks (Mountain vs. Forest) turns on that relative timestamp, and the layer rules governing that comparison weren't included in the context.

question: Aubriella controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], a [Sapseep Forest], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Sapseep Forest and Saproling look like?
answer:
Both end up identical: each is a 1/1 green Saproling Mountain — a nonbasic Land Creature — whose only ability is "{T}: Add {R}."

How that happens (CR 613 layers, timestamp order — Life and Limb entered before Blood Moon):

Layer 4 (types/subtypes):
- Life and Limb (timestamp 1) makes all Forests and all Saprolings both Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types. Sapseep Forest is a Forest, so it becomes a Land Creature — Forest Saproling; the Saproling token becomes a Land Creature — Forest Saproling too (subtypes stay correlated: Forest is the land type, Saproling the creature type, per [205.3c] and [Life and Limb ruling #3]).
- Blood Moon (timestamp 2) then applies to every nonbasic land, which by now includes both permanents (neither has the supertype "basic," [205.4c]). It makes them Mountains, stripping their other land types — so Forest is gone and Mountain replaces it ([Blood Moon ruling #2]).
- Because Blood Moon has removed the Forest subtype, Life and Limb no longer "sees" them as Forests/Forest-lands, but per [613.6] an effect that started applying in one layer keeps applying to the same objects in every other applicable layer — so Life and Limb's color and P/T parts still apply.

Layer 5 (color): Life and Limb makes both green.
Layer 6 (abilities): Blood Moon removes Sapseep Forest's abilities ("{T}: Add {G}", "This land enters tapped," and "{G}, {T}: You gain 1 life") and it gains the intrinsic Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}" from [305.6]/[107.4a].
Layer 7b: Life and Limb sets both to 1/1.

Practical notes: they're creatures, so they're subject to summoning sickness — you can't pay the {T} in "{T}: Add {R}" unless you've controlled them continuously since your turn began ([Life and Limb ruling #0]). Sapseep Forest's "enters tapped" clause is irrelevant now that it's on the battlefield (it applied on entry as a replacement effect, [614.1c]). Note {R} is red mana specifically, not generic {1} and not {G}. This is a purely board-state/layers question, so the answer is the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer.

question: Ainsley controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], a [Cinder Glade], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Cinder Glade and Saproling look like?
answer:
Cinder Glade is just a colorless nonbasic "Land — Mountain" that taps for {R} and is not a creature. The Saproling token is a 1/1 green "Creature Land — Saproling Forest" that taps for {G}.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.5, 613.6), applying in timestamp order Blood Moon (first) then Life and Limb (second):

Cinder Glade
- Layer 4: Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") applies first. Cinder Glade is nonbasic, so its land subtypes become just Mountain — it loses Forest (Blood Moon ruling #2, 205.3i).
- Layer 6: per Blood Moon ruling #2 it loses its other abilities, including "This land enters tapped unless you control two or more basic lands," and it has the intrinsic Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}" (305.6, 107.4a). Note {R} is specifically red mana, not generic.
- Life and Limb then finds nothing to work with: by the time it applies, Cinder Glade is neither a Forest nor a Saproling, so it doesn't become a 1/1 green Saproling creature at all. Its supertype status (nonbasic) is unchanged (205.4b).

Saproling token
- The token's copiable characteristics are only what created it: a 1/1 green Saproling creature with no abilities (111.3).
- Layer 4: when Blood Moon applies (earlier timestamp), the token is not a land, so Blood Moon does nothing to it. Then Life and Limb makes it a 1/1 green Saproling creature and Forest land in addition to its other types — card types Creature and Land, subtypes Saproling (creature type) and Forest (land type), each correlated to the right card type (205.3c, Life and Limb ruling #3).
- Because it now has the basic land type Forest, it has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {G}" (305.6). It's still a nonbasic land (it has no "Basic" supertype), but Blood Moon's effect was already applied and doesn't re-apply to it in this ordering, so it stays a Forest.
- It's affected by summoning sickness, so it can't tap for {G} or attack until it's been under Ainsley's control since their most recent turn began.

Timing assumption: the stated enter order is the timestamp order, Blood Moon before Life and Limb, and both are on the battlefield at the same time as the token. If Life and Limb had entered before Blood Moon, the order flips: Cinder Glade would first become a 1/1 green Saproling Forest creature land, and then Blood Moon would strip Forest and make it a Mountain (a 1/1 Saproling creature land that taps for {R}), and the Saproling token, having become a nonbasic land, would then be turned into a Mountain by Blood Moon and tap for {R} instead of {G}.

Player count doesn't matter here — these are static continuous effects affecting only Ainsley's own permanents, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Alannah controls [Ore-Rich Stalactite], [Life and Limb], [March of the Machines], and [Xenograft] naming "Saproling", that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Ore-Rich Stalactite?
answer:
Ore-Rich Stalactite ends up as a 1/1 green Saproling Forest artifact creature — an artifact land creature that also still has its own printed abilities.

How it gets there, layer by layer:

**Layer 4 (types/subtypes), applied in timestamp order:**
- March of the Machines makes each noncreature artifact an artifact creature, so Ore-Rich Stalactite becomes an artifact creature.
- Xenograft (naming Saproling) makes each creature you control that type in addition to its others, so Ore-Rich Stalactite is now a Saproling. (Xenograft depends on March of the Machines having made it a creature; the timestamp order given already applies them that way.)
- Life and Limb says all Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types. Since Ore-Rich Stalactite is now a Saproling, Life and Limb also makes it a Forest land. So its types are artifact land creature — Saproling Forest — the artifact/land combination described under Artifact Land, subject to the rules for both.

**Layer 5 (color):** Life and Limb makes it green (it was otherwise colorless as an artifact).

**Layer 7b (setting power/toughness):** March of the Machines sets it to its mana value, 2/2; Life and Limb sets it to 1/1. Life and Limb has the later timestamp, so the final result is 1/1. Note that per rule 613.6, March of the Machines keeps applying its power/toughness part to the same object even though that object is no longer a "noncreature artifact" by layer 7b — it's just overwritten by the later effect.

**Abilities:** Because it has the basic land type Forest, it has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {G}" (rule 305.6) — that's {G}, green mana, not the {R} from its own ability. It also keeps its printed "{T}: Add {R}. Spend this mana only to cast an instant or sorcery spell" and its Craft ability. Since it's now a creature, summoning sickness applies to tapping it for either mana ability unless it has been under Alannah's control since her most recent turn began.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Ainsley controls [Furycalm Snarl], [Humility], [Magus of the Moon], and [Crosis's Catacombs] that entered the battlefield in that order. What are the characteristics of the Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs?
answer:
Direct answer: both Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs are colorless nonbasic Lands whose only land subtype is Mountain, and each taps for {R}. Humility does not change them at all, because Humility only affects creatures and neither land is a creature.

Why Magus of the Moon still works even though Humility is on the battlefield first: continuous effects are applied in layers (CR 613.1). Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" is a type-changing effect, applied in layer 4. Humility's "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1" is applied in layer 6 (ability removal) and layer 7b (base P/T), which come after layer 4. So when layer 4 is applied, Magus of the Moon's ability is still there and its land-type effect applies; Humility then strips Magus of the Moon's abilities in layer 6 and makes it a 1/1, but that doesn't retroactively undo the layer-4 land-type change (CR 613.6 also confirms an effect that has started applying keeps applying).

Resulting characteristics:
- Furycalm Snarl: Land — Mountain, nonbasic, colorless, mana value 0. Being a Mountain gives it "{T}: Add {R}" (the glossary Swamp entry states the parallel rule: any land with that basic land subtype has the corresponding mana ability). Its printed "As this land enters, you may reveal a Mountain or Plains card..." ability is a replacement effect that already finished doing its job as it entered (CR 614.1c), so it's irrelevant now; whether it's tapped or untapped is unchanged.
- Crosis's Catacombs: Land — Mountain, nonbasic, colorless, mana value 0, with "{T}: Add {R}". It is no longer a Lair. Its enters-the-battlefield sacrifice trigger already triggered and resolved when it entered (it entered after Magus of the Moon, so at that time it was already a Mountain, not a Lair, and it could itself have been the "non-Lair land" returned only if you chose another permanent — practically you had to return some non-Lair land you control or sacrifice it; that's already resolved history).

One caveat about grounding: the general rule that a land which becomes a basic land type loses its previous land types and rules text and gains the corresponding mana ability (CR 305.7) was not included in the provided context; I'm relying on the glossary Swamp entry's statement that any land with a basic land subtype has that subtype's mana ability, plus Magus of the Moon's own text. Under that, the lands' original mana abilities ({R}/{W} and {U}/{B}/{R}) are replaced by "{T}: Add {R}".

Multiplayer: nothing here depends on the number of players — Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands and Humility affects all creatures regardless of controller, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
No — Volrath's Shapeshifter does not have flying in this situation.

Why: Volrath's Shapeshifter says that as long as the top card of your graveyard is a creature card, it has the "full text" of that card plus the text "{2}: Discard a card." Per [612.6], "full text" changes not just the text box and type line but also the name, mana cost, color indicator, power, and toughness. So it would normally pick up Mistform Skyreaver's name, mana cost, color, types, 6/6 body, and Mistform Skyreaver's abilities (Flying and "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn").

But Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." A card's own printed text controls here, and Mistform Skyreaver is a card in a graveyard, so it currently has no abilities at all. There is no flying text on it to copy. What Volrath's Shapeshifter takes on is the text of the card as it exists — a Mistform Skyreaver with an empty ability set. The only exception is a characteristic-defining ability like changeling, which still functions from the graveyard per [Yixlid Jailer ruling #1]; flying is a normal static keyword ability ([702.9a], [Flying]), not a CDA, so it is stripped.

Result: Aiden's Volrath's Shapeshifter is a 6/6 blue creature named Mistform Skyreaver, Creature — Illusion, with mana cost {5}{U}{U}, whose only ability is the granted "{2}: Discard a card" ([Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1] — it keeps the granted ability in addition to those of the copied card). Without flying it can be blocked by any creature ([702.9b]).

Timing note: this is a static, continuously-checked condition. If Yixlid Jailer leaves the battlefield (or stops applying) while Mistform Skyreaver is still the top card of the graveyard, Mistform Skyreaver regains its abilities and Volrath's Shapeshifter immediately gains flying and the {1} type-changing ability.

Player count doesn't matter here: Yixlid Jailer affects cards in all graveyards, and none of the rules involved depend on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Nickolas controls [Dryad Arbor]. Aniya casts [Overwhelming Splendor], enchanting Nickolas. After it resolves, can Nickolas tap the Dryad Arbor for {G}?
answer:
No. Nickolas can't tap Dryad Arbor for {G} while Overwhelming Splendor enchants him.

Why: Dryad Arbor is a Land Creature — Forest Dryad, so it is a creature Nickolas controls. Overwhelming Splendor says "Creatures enchanted player controls lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Dryad Arbor's mana ability "{T}: Add {G}" is not printed text — it's the intrinsic ability every object with the Forest basic land type has (305.6). Intrinsic or not, it's an ability, and the layer-6 ability-removal effect strips it; Dryad Arbor keeps the Forest subtype but has no abilities at all (its P/T is set to 1/1 in layer 7b). Running the layers confirms: after Overwhelming Splendor, Dryad Arbor is a green Land Creature — Forest Dryad, 1/1, with an empty ability list. With no {T} ability to activate, there is nothing to tap it for.

Two side notes: (1) Overwhelming Splendor's second clause, "Enchanted player can't activate abilities that aren't mana abilities or loyalty abilities," would have let a mana ability through — but that's moot, because the ability no longer exists to be activated. Note also that a mana ability stays a mana ability even when it can't produce mana (605.2); here the ability itself is gone, which is different. (2) Per the Overwhelming Splendor ruling, if some effect grants Dryad Arbor an ability after Overwhelming Splendor became attached (for example, an effect giving it "{T}: Add {G}" again, or turning it into a land that isn't a creature so the Aura stops applying to it), it would keep that new ability and could tap for mana then.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — Overwhelming Splendor enchants one specific player, so at a multiplayer table only Nickolas's creatures are affected, and other players' Dryad Arbors tap for {G} normally.

question: Nico controls [Yixlid Jailer]. Achilles uses [Past in Flames] to give [Deadly Complication] in their graveyard Flashback. Is Achilles able to cast Deadly Complication from their graveyard to destroy Yixlid Jailer?
answer:
No. With Nico's Yixlid Jailer on the battlefield, Achilles can't cast Deadly Complication from the graveyard, so it can't be used to destroy Yixlid Jailer.

Why: Past in Flames gives each instant and sorcery card in Achilles's graveyard flashback until end of turn (flashback cost equal to its mana cost, here {1}{B}{R}). Flashback is a static ability that functions while the card is in a player's graveyard and permits casting it from there [702.34a], and abilities granted to the card are abilities the card has. Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," which strips that granted flashback ability off Deadly Complication while it sits in the graveyard. The Yixlid Jailer ruling is explicit: when a card's own ability (such as a flashback ability) is what allows you to cast it from your graveyard, Yixlid Jailer stops that ability [Yixlid Jailer ruling #0]. By contrast, if a separate spell or ability itself said "cast target card from your graveyard," that permission comes from elsewhere and would still work; Past in Flames does not do that — it only grants an ability to the card [Yixlid Jailer ruling #0].

Timing note: I'm assuming Past in Flames already resolved while Yixlid Jailer was on the battlefield and Yixlid Jailer is still there when Achilles wants to cast Deadly Complication. Past in Flames resolving is fine either way — the grant happens, it's just continuously turned off in the graveyard. If Yixlid Jailer leaves the battlefield (or is destroyed by something else) later in the same turn, Deadly Complication regains the granted flashback and Achilles could then cast it for {1}{B}{R}, subject to sorcery timing [Past in Flames ruling #10] and it will be exiled afterward [Past in Flames ruling #9]. Also note Past in Flames only affects cards in the graveyard as it resolves [Past in Flames ruling #3].

Multiplayer: this answer is the same regardless of player count — Yixlid Jailer affects all graveyards, not just its controller's. Targeting Yixlid Jailer, a permanent an opponent controls, would be committing a crime [700.13], which matters only for cards that care about crimes.

answer_gold: Yes. Both Yixlid Jailer and Past in Flames are applying a continuous effect to Deadly Complication, and both are being applied in layer 6. Since there is no dependency between the two effects, they are applied in timestamp order; Yixlid Jailer removes all abilities from Deadly Complication, which is then given flashback by Past in Flames.

question: Aspen controls [Watchwolf] enchanted by [Lignify], [Figure of Destiny] that's had its third ability activated, and [Swab Goblin]. They casts [Pack's Favor] targeting Swab Goblin. After that resolves, they casts [Mirrorweave] targeting Figure of Destiny. What are the characteristics of Swab Goblin and Watchwolf?
answer:
Direct answer: Swab Goblin becomes a 4/4 red-and-white Creature — Kithkin named Figure of Destiny with Figure of Destiny's three activated abilities (1/1 base, +3/+3 from Pack's Favor). Watchwolf becomes a 0/4 red-and-white Creature — Treefolk named Figure of Destiny with no abilities, because Lignify keeps applying on top of the copy.

Why:

1. Mirrorweave's copy effect applies in layer 1 (CR 613.1a, 613.2a). What gets copied are only Figure of Destiny's copiable values — the values derived from its printed text: name Figure of Destiny, mana cost {R/W} (hence red and white), Creature — Kithkin, 1/1, and its three activated abilities (CR 707.2a, 707.3). Crucially, the fact that Aspen activated the third ability, making Figure of Destiny an 8/8 Kithkin Spirit Warrior Avatar with flying and first strike, is NOT copied: that's a type-changing/base-P/T-setting continuous effect in layers 4/7b, and "other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied" (CR 707.2a). So the copies are 1/1 Kithkin, not 8/8 Avatars. Figure of Destiny itself is unaffected by Mirrorweave ("each other creature") and stays an 8/8 Kithkin Spirit Warrior Avatar with flying and first strike.

2. Swab Goblin: after layer 1 it is a 1/1 red-and-white Kithkin named Figure of Destiny with the three {R/W} activated abilities. Pack's Favor's +3/+3 is a layer 7c effect that still applies (it wasn't copied away; only copiable values changed), giving 4/4 (CR 613.1a, 613.7). Note Swab Goblin can now activate the first ability for {R/W}, but the second/third check whether it's already a Spirit/Warrior.

3. Watchwolf: Lignify is still attached (Mirrorweave doesn't remove Auras) and its effects apply after layer 1: layer 4 makes it a Treefolk (replacing Kithkin), layer 6 removes all abilities — including the copied Figure of Destiny activated abilities — and layer 7b sets base power/toughness 0/4. Result: a 0/4 red-and-white Creature — Treefolk named Figure of Destiny with no abilities. Lignify's overwriting of copied P/T-defining and type-defining text is consistent with Lignify ruling #5.

Both conclusions are timestamp-driven; nothing here creates a dependency (CR 613.8).

Assumption on timing: I'm reading it as Pack's Favor fully resolving before Mirrorweave is cast, as stated. If instead Mirrorweave resolved first and Pack's Favor afterward, the end result for Swab Goblin would be identical (4/4), since layer 7c always applies after the layer 1 copy.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players — Mirrorweave affects each other creature on the battlefield regardless of controller, so in a multiplayer game every other creature at the table (not just Aspen's) becomes a copy of Figure of Destiny too.

question: Allison controls [Dralnu's Crusade] and [Leopard-Spotted Jiao]. Allison then casts [Conspiracy] naming "Goblin". What are the creature types of Leopard-Spotted Jiao and does it get +1/+1?
answer:
Leopard-Spotted Jiao ends up as a Goblin Zombie, it's black instead of red, and yes, it gets +1/+1, making it a 4/2.

Why: Conspiracy (the enchantment) sets the creature types of creatures Allison controls to the chosen type, Goblin, and per [Conspiracy ruling #4] affected creatures lose all their other creature types \u2014 so Leopard-Spotted Jiao loses Beast and is just a Goblin. Both Conspiracy's type-setting and Dralnu's Crusade's "are Zombies in addition to their other creature types" apply in the type-changing layer (CR 613 layer 4). Dralnu's Crusade's effect depends on Conspiracy's, because applying Conspiracy changes whether Leopard-Spotted Jiao is something Dralnu's Crusade applies to; so Conspiracy applies first even though Dralnu's Crusade has the earlier timestamp. Result in that layer: Goblin Zombie. Note Conspiracy only changes the type line \u2014 it doesn't rewrite the word "Goblin" in other cards' text ([Conspiracy ruling #0]), so Dralnu's Crusade still looks for actual Goblins, and Leopard-Spotted Jiao now is one.

Color and P/T follow: in the color layer, Dralnu's Crusade makes all Goblins black \u2014 black only, not black in addition to red ([Dralnu's Crusade ruling #0]). In the power/toughness modification layer, the +1/+1 applies to the 3/1 body, giving 4/2.

Subtypes are the words after the dash on the type line, and creature subtypes are creature types (CR 205.3a, 205.3b, 205.3m, 302.3). Nothing here turns on player count: Conspiracy and Dralnu's Crusade only affect Allison's own Goblins, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

gold_text.613.8a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. An effect is said to “depend on” another if (a) it’s applied in the same layer (and, if applicable, sublayer) as the other effect; (b) applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to; and (c) neither effect is from a characteristic-defining ability or both effects are from characteristic-defining abilities. Otherwise, the effect is considered to be independent of the other effect.
gold_text.613.8b: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. An effect dependent on one or more other effects waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied. If multiple dependent effects would apply simultaneously in this way, they’re applied in timestamp order relative to each other. If several dependent effects form a dependency loop, then this rule is ignored and the effects in the dependency loop are applied in timestamp order.

question: Alaina has seven cards in their hand and controls [Recycle]. They cast [Trusted Advisor]. After that resolves, what is Alaina's maximum hand size?
answer:
Alaina's maximum hand size is four.

Maximum hand size is the number of cards a player must discard down to during their cleanup step; it's normally seven [402.2]. Effects that modify it are applied in timestamp order. Recycle sets Alaina's maximum hand size to two, and Trusted Advisor, entering the battlefield later, then increases it by two, for a total of four [Trusted Advisor ruling #0], [Recycle ruling #2]. If the permanents had entered in the opposite order (Trusted Advisor first, then Recycle), Recycle's later setting effect would win and the maximum hand size would be two.

Alaina's current seven cards in hand are fine right now — maximum hand size only matters as the cleanup step of their turn begins, at which point the active player discards down to that number as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [514.1], [703.4n], [Recycle ruling #1]. So on Alaina's next cleanup step, with a maximum hand size of four, they'd discard down to four cards. Note also that Recycle's "Whenever you play a card, draw a card" and Trusted Advisor's upkeep trigger will change how many cards are in hand before then.

This works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; maximum hand size is per-player and isn't affected by the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

All such effects are applied in timestamp order after the determination of objects’ characteristics. See also the rules for timestamp order and dependency (rules 613.7 and 613.8).
gold_text.613.7: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp.

cited_text.402.2: Each player has a maximum hand size, which is normally seven cards. A player may have any number of cards in their hand, but as part of their cleanup step, the player must discard excess cards down to the maximum hand size.

question: Alisson controls [Quickening Licid], [March of the Machines], and [Mycosynth Lattice] that entered the battlefield in that order. They activate Quickening Licid's ability targeting itself. What happens?
answer:
Quickening Licid ends up in Alisson's graveyard. 

Step by step:

1. Alisson activates Quickening Licid's ability ({1}{W}, {T}) targeting Quickening Licid itself. At that moment Quickening Licid is a creature (it's a Licid creature, and Mycosynth Lattice also makes it an artifact), so it's a legal target.

2. On resolution, Quickening Licid loses that activated ability and becomes an Aura enchantment with enchant creature, and tries to attach to the target — itself.

3. Layers: characteristic-defining and continuous effects are applied in layers, with type-changing effects in layer 4 (rules 613.1a, 613.6). Mycosynth Lattice makes Quickening Licid an artifact in addition to its other types. Because Quickening Licid is now an Aura enchantment artifact and (after its own effect) not a creature, March of the Machines' static ability applies to it: "Each noncreature artifact is an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value." Quickening Licid's mana value is 2, so it becomes a 2/2 Aura enchantment artifact creature.

4. An Aura that is also a creature can't enchant anything (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3). So Quickening Licid can't legally be attached — and an Aura couldn't enchant itself in any case. The next time state-based actions are checked, Quickening Licid is unattached, and then, as a second state-based action, an Aura attached to nothing is put into its owner's graveyard.

So the net result of the activation is that Alisson pays {1}{W}, taps Quickening Licid, and loses it to the graveyard. Note Quickening Licid's ability also says "You may pay {W} to end this effect" — if Alisson pays {W} in response to/at the time state-based actions haven't yet been performed, that isn't possible here, because state-based actions are checked before any player receives priority again after the ability resolves; Alisson gets no window to pay {W} first.

This outcome doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?
answer:
Duplicant is a 4/4 (and an Artifact Creature — Shapeshifter Zombie Elemental).

Why: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's third ability says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is neither hand nor library, so all three +1/+1 counters stay on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card in exile (Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5, ruling #1 — the ability works because Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had it in the zone it left, the battlefield). Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text overrides the general expectation that counters fall off on a zone change.

A +1/+1 counter on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield still adds to that card's power and toughness ([122.1a]), and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2 confirms exactly this (a Skullbriar, the Walking Grave with one counter in the command zone is 2/2). So the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is 1/1 base plus three counters = 4/4.

Duplicant's static ability then gives Duplicant "the power, toughness, and creature types of the last creature card exiled with it," so Duplicant's base 2/4 is overwritten in layer 7b ([613.1g], [613.4a] for the layer-7 sublayer framework) with 4/4, and it gains Zombie and Elemental while staying a Shapeshifter. Duplicant ruling #0 notes Duplicant's base power/toughness change to the imprinted card's, and any counters or effects on Duplicant itself would still apply on top (there are none here).

Note the limit in Duplicant ruling #2: characteristic-defining abilities that define a * apply in exile, but abilities that add or subtract power/toughness don't. Counters are not such an ability — they're markers that modify the card's power and toughness directly ([122.1a]), so they do count.

One timing note: this assumes the counters were on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave when it was exiled. If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had somehow lost its counter-retention ability before leaving the battlefield (e.g., an effect stripping its abilities, per Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1), the counters would vanish and Duplicant would be 1/1 instead.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players; the same result holds in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can cast Murder targeting Pristine Angel.

Why: Pristine Angel's protection is conditional ("As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color"), so while Pristine Angel was tapped and attacking it had no protection at all, and Cephalid Snitch's ability legally targeted it. That ability resolved and created a continuous effect lasting until end of turn: Pristine Angel loses protection from black. Nothing about untapping ends that effect — it has a later timestamp than Pristine Angel's own static ability, so when Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel, Pristine Angel regains protection from artifacts and from every color except black. Murder is a black instant, so it can target and destroy Pristine Angel.

Two side notes: untapping Pristine Angel does not remove it from combat — tapping or untapping a creature already declared as an attacker doesn't remove it from combat or prevent its combat damage [506.4b]. And if Murder is on the stack and Pristine Angel somehow regained protection from black before Murder resolved, Pristine Angel would be an illegal target and Murder would be removed from the stack without resolving [608.2b]; that isn't the case here.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability fully resolved before Abel cast the spell, as stated. If instead Cephalid Snitch's ability were still on the stack when Pristine Angel untapped, Pristine Angel would then have protection from blue and the Cephalid Snitch ability would have an illegal target and do nothing [608.2b], leaving Pristine Angel untargetable by Murder.

Player count doesn't change any of this; the provided rules here are not player-count dependent, though note that targeting an opponent's permanent is a "crime" for cards that care about that [700.13].

question: Alijah controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Alijah then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
answer:
Badlands taps for white mana only — {W}.

Why: both Conversion ("All Mountains are Plains") and Magus of the Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") are type-changing continuous effects that apply in layer 4. Normally they'd be applied in timestamp order, but Conversion depends on Magus of the Moon: whether Conversion applies to Badlands at all, and what it does to it, is changed by applying Magus of the Moon first. So Magus of the Moon is applied first.

Step 1 — Magus of the Moon: Badlands is a nonbasic land, so its subtypes are set to just Mountain. It loses Swamp (and thus loses "{T}: Add {B}") and gains "{T}: Add {R}" [305.7, Magus of the Moon ruling #4].

Step 2 — Conversion: Badlands is now a Mountain, so Conversion makes it a Plains. Setting the subtype again removes Mountain and the red mana ability, and Badlands gains the intrinsic Plains ability "{T}: Add {W}" [305.6, 305.7, Conversion ruling #0].

So the Swamp/Mountain dual that used to add {B} or {R} [Badlands ruling #3] now adds only {W}. Note Conversion and Magus of the Moon don't touch supertypes or the card's name [Conversion ruling #1, Magus of the Moon ruling #1], and Badlands remains nonbasic, so Magus of the Moon keeps applying to it. Note also {W} is white mana specifically, not generic mana.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players — both effects apply to all Mountains/nonbasic lands regardless of controller, so the result is the same in two-player and multiplayer games. I'm assuming Magus of the Moon has resolved and is on the battlefield with both effects active; if Magus of the Moon were removed, Conversion would no longer see Badlands as a Mountain and Badlands would revert to adding {B} or {R}.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip resolves, Wandering Ones has flying (and haste), and is a -5/1 creature.

Why: Fleetfeather Sandals and Tightening Coils both produce continuous effects in layer 6 (ability adding/removing), so they're ordered by timestamp [613.1f, 613.7a]. Neither depends on the other; the later one simply wins [613.9]. An Equipment receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object [613.7e], so re-activating Fleetfeather Sandals's Equip {2} and attaching it again to Wandering Ones gives its "Equipped creature has flying and haste" ability a timestamp later than Tightening Coils. Applying in order: Tightening Coils removes flying, then Fleetfeather Sandals grants flying and haste — so Wandering Ones ends up with flying. This matches Tightening Coils ruling #0: if an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached, the creature has flying.

Tightening Coils's -6/-0 applies in layer 7c regardless, so Wandering Ones is 1-6 = -5 power, 1 toughness (a negative power counts as 0 for dealing damage purposes). Multiple instances of flying would be redundant anyway [702.9c].

Note that Equip only works as a sorcery and can be activated even if Fleetfeather Sandals is already attached to that same creature; re-attaching it is what refreshes the timestamp [702.6d, 604.4]. Player count doesn't matter here — the same layer ordering applies in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Tightening Coils became attached before the equip activation, as stated. If instead Fleetfeather Sandals had been attached last before Tightening Coils and never re-equipped, Tightening Coils would have the later timestamp and Wandering Ones would not have flying.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Soldevi Digger ends up as a colorless 2/2 artifact creature — Equipment with no abilities at all.

How the layers get there (CR 613.1a, 613.6, 613.7 — same timestamp order in each layer, no dependency applies):

- Layer 4 (types/subtypes): Bludgeon Brawl has the earlier timestamp, so it applies first and makes Soldevi Digger an Equipment (it qualified: at that point it was a noncreature, non-Equipment artifact). Then Titania's Song makes it an artifact creature. Result: Artifact Creature — Equipment.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Bludgeon Brawl first grants "equip {2}" and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0" (X = Soldevi Digger's mana value, which is 2 — that's {2} generic to equip). Then Titania's Song, with the later timestamp, removes all abilities — including Soldevi Digger's printed "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library" and the two abilities Bludgeon Brawl just granted. Result: no abilities.
- Layer 7b: Titania's Song sets power and toughness each equal to mana value, so 2/2. Note the mana value used is still 2 ({2} generic on the printed card); Bludgeon Brawl doesn't change mana cost.
- Color: nothing changes it, so Soldevi Digger stays colorless (CR 105.2 — no colored mana symbols in its cost, no color indicator or color-defining ability).

Key point about CR 613.6: once Bludgeon Brawl's effect starts applying in layer 4, it keeps applying to Soldevi Digger in layer 6 even though by then Soldevi Digger is a creature and an Equipment — but its granted abilities are stripped anyway because Titania's Song's ability-removal has the later timestamp.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Bludgeon Brawl was already on the battlefield before Titania's Song resolved (as stated). If instead Titania's Song had the earlier timestamp, Bludgeon Brawl would then no longer apply — Soldevi Digger would be a creature, and Bludgeon Brawl only affects noncreature artifacts — so it would be a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities and no Equipment subtype. Also, if Titania's Song later leaves the battlefield, its own text says the effect continues until end of turn.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; both cards affect artifacts regardless of controller, and the provided rules contain nothing player-count-specific here.

question: Ariah controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nickolas casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
answer:
Wayward Angel becomes a 4/4 blue Frog creature with no abilities, controlled by Ariah.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1g, 613.7):

- Layer 4 (types): Turn to Frog makes Wayward Angel a Frog, replacing Angel Horror. It's still a creature.
- Layer 5 (color): Wayward Angel's threshold ability (earlier timestamp) makes it black — and only black, not white and black [Wayward Angel ruling #0]. Then Turn to Frog (later timestamp) makes it blue, overwriting that. Final: blue only.
- Layer 6 (abilities): The threshold ability applies first (timestamp order), granting trample and the upkeep sacrifice trigger; then Turn to Frog removes all abilities. Final: no abilities at all (no flying, no vigilance, no trample, no threshold trigger).
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1, overwriting the printed 4/4 [Turn to Frog ruling #0].
- Layer 7c (P/T modification): This is the key point. Under CR 613.6, an effect that has already started to apply in one layer continues to apply in every other applicable layer even though the ability generating it was removed. The threshold effect already started applying back in layer 5, so its +3/+3 still applies in layer 7c even though the ability itself was stripped in layer 6. 1/1 + 3/+3 = 4/4.

So the result is a 4/4 blue Frog creature named Wayward Angel with no abilities. Note this depends on Ariah still having seven or more cards in their graveyard; the threshold condition is checked continuously, and if the graveyard drops below seven the +3/+3 (and the black color, already overwritten anyway) stops applying and Wayward Angel becomes 1/1. This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players — it's the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since Turn to Frog just targets one creature. Also, if Wayward Angel later gains an ability from a new effect, it keeps it [Turn to Frog ruling #3]. All of this lasts until end of turn.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
Afterward Wayward Angel is a 1/1 black Frog creature named Wayward Angel with no abilities.

How we get there:

1. Manifested = face down: while face down it was a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, or abilities and no mana cost, and those are its copiable values ([708.2], [708.2a], [613.2b]).
2. Turn to Frog resolved on it: "Until end of turn, target creature loses all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1." That's a continuous effect with a single timestamp applying in layer 4 (type/subtype), layer 5 (color), layer 6 (lose all abilities), and layer 7b (base 1/1).
3. Turning it face up changes its copiable values back to the printed Wayward Angel values ([708.8], [708.10], [707.2]) — but Turn to Frog's effect keeps applying to the permanent, since 708.8 says any effects already applied to the face-down permanent still apply to the face-up permanent. Its own "enters the battlefield" abilities don't trigger ([708.8]).
4. Now apply layers ([613.1], [613.1g], [613.7]) to the newly-restored base 4/4 white Angel Horror with flying, vigilance, and Threshold:
   - Layer 4: Turn to Frog makes it just a Frog creature (Angel and Horror are gone; it would keep any other card types/supertypes — it has none) [Turn to Frog ruling #1].
   - Layer 5: Turn to Frog (earlier timestamp) makes it blue; then the Threshold ability — which still exists in layer 5, because abilities aren't removed until layer 6 — makes it black. It is black only, not white-and-black [Wayward Angel ruling #0]. This is the same ordering principle as [Turn to Frog ruling #4]: the creature's own ability applies in the earlier layer before the ability-removal in layer 6.
   - Layer 6: Turn to Frog removes all abilities — flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability itself all go away.
   - Layer 7b: base power/toughness set to 1/1 [Turn to Frog ruling #0]. The Threshold +3/+3 would be layer 7c, but by then the Threshold ability no longer exists, so it doesn't apply, and there's no upkeep sacrifice trigger or trample either.

Timing assumption: Turn to Frog fully resolved before the face-up special action, as stated. If instead Wayward Angel were turned face up first and Turn to Frog resolved after, the end result would be the same characteristics (Turn to Frog would still have the later timestamp in layer 5, so it would be blue rather than black — that's the one difference: blue 1/1 Frog with no abilities).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it's the same with two players or more. Note also that if Turn to Frog's effect ends at end of turn while the permanent is face up, Wayward Angel goes back to being a 4/4 white Angel Horror with its printed abilities (and Threshold would then make it a 7/7 black trampler with the upkeep sacrifice trigger while seven or more cards are in Ariella's graveyard).

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its only creature type is Ferret. Its full type line ends up as "Legendary Land Creature — Swamp Ferret" (Swamp is a land type, Ferret the creature type), and it's a 6/4 green creature.

How it gets there, working through the type-changing effects in timestamp order:

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability makes each land a Swamp in addition to its other land types, including itself while it's on the battlefield ([Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #2]).
2. Kormus Bell then sees a Swamp: "All Swamps are 1/1 black creatures that are still lands," so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth becomes a land creature and keeps its land types and its Legendary supertype ([205.1b], [205.4b], [Kormus Bell ruling #0]).
3. Vastwood Zendikon makes the enchanted land a 6/4 green Elemental creature that's still a land ([Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5]). Since it's later than Kormus Bell, it sets the color to green and the power/toughness to 6/4.
4. Conspiracy, though it entered first, has to be applied after the others in the type-changing layer: it only affects creatures Ahmad controls, and whether Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature at all is determined by Kormus Bell and Vastwood Zendikon. Applying Conspiracy last, it sets the creature type to the chosen type, Ferret, and the permanent loses all other creature types — so the Elemental type from Vastwood Zendikon is gone ([Conspiracy ruling #4]). Conspiracy can grant a creature type to animated lands that would otherwise have none ([Conspiracy ruling #1]).

Notes: Conspiracy changes only creature types, so the land type Swamp ([205.3c] — subtypes correlate to the card type they belong to) and the Legendary supertype ([205.4b]) both remain. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth still has all its card types (land and creature) and satisfies anything that cares about either ([205.2b]). Conspiracy also doesn't rewrite creature-type words in card text ([Conspiracy ruling #0]).

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since all four permanents are Ahmad's.

question: Andre controls [Raugrin Triome] and [Prismatic Omen]. Nala casts [Blood Moon]. After it resolves, what land types does Raugrin Triome have?
answer:
Raugrin Triome ends up with just one land type: Mountain. Its only ability is the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}" from that Mountain type.

Why: both Prismatic Omen and Blood Moon are type-changing continuous effects, applied in layer 4 in timestamp order. Prismatic Omen (older) first makes Raugrin Triome every basic land type — Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest, on top of its own Island/Mountain/Plains. Then Blood Moon resolves (newer timestamp) and says nonbasic lands are Mountains, which sets the land's types to Mountain and removes all other land types and abilities it had, giving it "{T}: Add {R}" (Blood Moon ruling #2). There's no dependency that reverses this order: Prismatic Omen doesn't change whether Blood Moon applies to Raugrin Triome, because Raugrin Triome is still nonbasic — adding basic land types does not add the "basic" supertype (Prismatic Omen ruling #1, Blood Moon ruling #1, rule 205.4 via "Nonbasic Land"/"Basic" glossary). So Prismatic Omen's contribution is simply overwritten.

Raugrin Triome keeps its name and any supertypes (it has none); it is still not a basic land. It also loses Cycling {3} and its "enters tapped" ability going forward, since Blood Moon strips its abilities.

Note the timing assumption: this is after Blood Moon has resolved, i.e., Blood Moon's timestamp is later than Prismatic Omen's. If instead Prismatic Omen were to enter the battlefield after Blood Moon, Prismatic Omen would apply last and add all five basic land types back, leaving Raugrin Triome as Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest (able to tap for {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}), though it still wouldn't get back Cycling {3}.

Player count doesn't matter here: Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer table.

question: Ariel controls [Frostboil Snarl] and [Blood Moon]. They cast [Prismatic Omen]. After it resolves, what land types does Frostboil Snarl have?
answer:
Frostboil Snarl has all five basic land types: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest.

Why: Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," and Frostboil Snarl is nonbasic (it has no "basic" supertype, CR 205.4c). Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type makes it lose its old land types and the abilities from its rules text, and gain the mana ability for the new type (CR 305.7; Blood Moon ruling #2) — so its printed "{T}: Add {U} or {R}" and its enters-tapped ability are gone. Note Frostboil Snarl printed has no land subtypes of its own anyway (Frostboil Snarl ruling #0).

Prismatic Omen then says lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types. Adding land types doesn't remove existing ones (CR 305.7, last sentence; Prismatic Omen ruling #0), so on top of Mountain from Blood Moon it also has Plains, Island, Swamp, and Forest. Both are type-changing effects in the same layer (CR 613 layer 4) applied in timestamp order, with Blood Moon first and Prismatic Omen second; neither depends on the other, and the result is the same set of types either way, since Blood Moon's setting effect would still be overlaid by Omen's addition.

Resulting mana abilities: from its five basic land types it has "{T}: Add {W}," "{T}: Add {U}," "{T}: Add {B}," "{T}: Add {R}," and "{T}: Add {G}" (CR 305.6, and the Plains/Island/Swamp/Mountain entries). It does not get back its original "{T}: Add {U} or {R}" ability — Blood Moon's effect stripped the rules-text abilities and continues to apply in the ability layer.

Supertypes and name are untouched: Frostboil Snarl is still named Frostboil Snarl and is still a nonbasic land (Blood Moon ruling #1, Prismatic Omen ruling #1, CR 205.4c).

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; Prismatic Omen only affects lands Ariel controls, while Blood Moon affects every nonbasic land at the table regardless of player count.

question: Adan restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. Adan puts [Blood Moon], [Prismatic Omen] and [Winged Temple of Orazca] onto the battlefield with Karn Liberated. What colors of mana can Winged Temple of Orazca tap for?
answer:
Direct answer: it depends on which of Blood Moon and Prismatic Omen has the later timestamp, and either way Winged Temple of Orazca loses its printed "{T}: Add one mana of any color" ability.

- If Blood Moon's type-setting applies first and Prismatic Omen's applies after: Winged Temple of Orazca is a Mountain Plains Island Swamp Forest, so it has the intrinsic mana abilities of all five basic land types and can tap for {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} (one mana, your choice of the five) [305.6, Prismatic Omen ruling #0].
- If Prismatic Omen's applies first and Blood Moon's applies after: Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" overwrites the subtypes entirely, leaving only Mountain, so Winged Temple of Orazca taps for {R} only [Blood Moon ruling #2, Mountain, 305.6].

Why the printed ability is gone in both cases: Blood Moon makes nonbasic lands Mountains and, per Blood Moon ruling #2, they lose their other land types and their abilities and gain "{T}: Add {R}." Winged Temple of Orazca is a nonbasic land, so both its "{T}: Add one mana of any color" ability and its {1}{G}{U}, {T} pump ability are stripped. The mana it can still produce comes purely from the intrinsic abilities granted by its basic land types under [305.6] ({W} for Plains, {U} for Island, {B} for Swamp, {R} for Mountain, {G} for Forest) — those are intrinsic to having the type, so Prismatic Omen's types re-grant them even though Blood Moon removed printed abilities [Prismatic Omen ruling #0].

Timing assumption: because Karn Liberated's −14 puts Blood Moon, Prismatic Omen and Winged Temple of Orazca onto the battlefield at the same time, the two enchantments' continuous effects have simultaneous timestamps; the provided rules don't include the tiebreaker rule for simultaneous timestamps, so I've given both outcomes. In practice the usual result players expect from Blood Moon plus Prismatic Omen when Prismatic Omen is later is all five colors. If instead one enchantment clearly hit the battlefield later (say Prismatic Omen was cast afterward), use the matching branch above.

Note also that "any color" would only ever have meant one of the five colors anyway, never colorless [105.4, 105.1, 106.1a]. Nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table — both enchantments affect lands regardless of opponent count, and Prismatic Omen only affects lands Adan controls.

question: Apollo controls [Realmwright] naming "Island", [Arcane Adaptation] naming "Saproling", and [Life and Limb], which entered the battlefield in that order. What are the types and subtypes of Realmwright?
answer:
Realmwright ends up as a Land Creature — Vedalken Wizard Saproling Forest Island, and it's a 1/1 green creature.

How it gets there (all in CR 613 layer 4 for types/subtypes):

1. Arcane Adaptation (naming Saproling) makes creatures Apollo controls that type in addition to their other types, so Realmwright becomes a Vedalken Wizard Saproling.
2. Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." Because Realmwright is now a Saproling, Life and Limb applies: Realmwright gains the land card type and the land type Forest (keeping creature, Vedalken, Wizard, Saproling). Per [Life and Limb ruling #3], each subtype stays correlated to its proper card type — Forest is a land type, Saproling is a creature type (see also [205.3c]).
3. Realmwright's own ability, "Lands you control are the chosen type in addition to their other types" (Island chosen), now applies to Realmwright itself, since Realmwright is a land. Even though Realmwright's ability has the earliest timestamp, it's applied after Life and Limb's type-changing effect because it depends on it under CR 613.8a: applying Life and Limb changes what Realmwright's effect applies to. So Realmwright also gains the land type Island.

Other consequences: Life and Limb sets Realmwright's color to green (layer 5) and its power/toughness to 1/1 (layer 7b) — it's no longer blue. Having the basic land types Forest and Island, Realmwright has the intrinsic mana abilities "{T}: Add {G}" and "{T}: Add {U}" per [305.6] and the Island glossary entry, and it's subject to summoning sickness as a creature. It keeps its own Realmwright ability; nothing removes abilities here. No supertypes are gained or lost ([205.4b]), and "in addition to their other types" wording preserves all prior types ([205.1b]).

This analysis doesn't depend on the player count — Arcane Adaptation, Life and Limb, and Realmwright are evaluated the same way in two-player and multiplayer games (Realmwright and Arcane Adaptation only affect permanents Apollo controls; Life and Limb affects all Forests and Saprolings, including opponents').
