question: Ainsley controls [Leyline of Singularity] and [Awoken Demon] equipped with [Helm of the Host]. When the trigger from Helm of the Host resolves, will the created token be legendary?
answer:
Yes — the token will be legendary, and Ainsley will then have to apply the legend rule.

Why: Helm of the Host says the token "isn't legendary," and that exception is part of the token's copiable values ([Helm of the Host ruling #3]). But Leyline of Singularity is a separate continuous effect that says "All nonland permanents are legendary," and it applies to the token once the token is on the battlefield, on top of its copiable values. Adding the legendary supertype doesn't remove any other supertypes the token has [Leyline of Singularity ruling #0], and [205.4b] confirms supertypes are added/retained independently. So Helm of the Host's exception loses out here not because card text is being ignored, but because Leyline of Singularity re-applies the supertype afterward — exactly the situation described in [Leyline of Singularity ruling #2], where tokens Ainsley controls end up legendary.

Consequence: the token is a copy of Awoken Demon, so it has the same name as Awoken Demon. With both Awoken Demon and the token legendary and under Ainsley's control, the legend rule state-based action applies: Ainsley chooses one to keep and the other is put into its owner's graveyard [704.5j], [205.4d]. Note the token still gains haste from Helm of the Host, though that matters only if Ainsley keeps the token.

One assumption: I'm treating Ecstatic Awakener as already transformed to its Awoken Demon face when the Helm of the Host trigger resolves, so the copy is of Awoken Demon. If the permanent were on its Ecstatic Awakener face instead, the same analysis applies with the name Ecstatic Awakener.

Also note [Helm of the Host ruling #1]: if the equipped creature has left the battlefield when the trigger resolves, no token is created at all.

This outcome is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — the legend rule is applied per player, and only Ainsley's permanents are involved.

question: Addison controls [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove] and casts [Blood Moon]. What are the characteristics of [Snow-Covered Island], [Study Hall], [Dryad Arbor], and [Mountain] after Blood Moon resolves?
answer:
Direct answer: Snow-Covered Island and Mountain are unaffected by Blood Moon (they're basic lands) and keep Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's grant of all five basic land types, so they tap for any of {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}. Study Hall and Dryad Arbor are nonbasic, so Blood Moon (later timestamp, same layer 4) overwrites the land types Dryad of the Ilysian Grove gave them: they are Mountains with only "{T}: Add {R}."

Details per permanent (Dryad of the Ilysian Grove was already on the battlefield, so it has the earlier timestamp; Blood Moon applies second in layer 4 for type-changing and layer 6 for abilities):

1) Snow-Covered Island — Basic Snow Land — Island, plus Plains, Swamp, Mountain, Forest from Dryad of the Ilysian Grove. It is a basic land because it has the "basic" supertype [205.4c], so Blood Moon doesn't apply to it at all. Being every basic land type, it has the intrinsic mana abilities of each [305.6], i.e. "{T}: Add {W}", "{T}: Add {U}", "{T}: Add {B}", "{T}: Add {R}", "{T}: Add {G}". Snow is just a supertype with no function of its own [205.4g, Snow-Covered Island ruling #0].

2) Study Hall — Land — Mountain, no supertypes, and its only ability is "{T}: Add {R}" (from the Mountain land type, [305.6], [Mountain]). Blood Moon strips its other land types and abilities, so it loses "{T}: Add {C}" and the "{1}, {T}: Add one mana of any color…" ability, and it loses the four extra basic land types Dryad of the Ilysian Grove gave it [Blood Moon ruling #2]. It does not become basic and is not named Mountain [Blood Moon ruling #1, 205.4c].

3) Dryad Arbor — Land Creature — Mountain Dryad, 1/1, green (color indicator, applies in all zones) [Dryad Arbor ruling #3]. It stays a creature and keeps the creature type Dryad because Blood Moon only changes land types [205.3c, 205.3i, Dryad Arbor ruling #0, Dryad Arbor ruling #2]. It loses "{T}: Add {G}" and instead has "{T}: Add {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #2, 305.6]. Still nonbasic.

4) Mountain — Basic Land — Mountain plus Plains, Island, Swamp, Forest from Dryad of the Ilysian Grove; basic, so Blood Moon ignores it. It taps for any one of the five colors [305.6].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Dryad of the Ilysian Grove was on the battlefield before Blood Moon resolved. If Blood Moon were already out and Dryad of the Ilysian Grove entered afterward, the later Dryad of the Ilysian Grove effect would apply after Blood Moon in layer 4, so Study Hall and Dryad Arbor would then have all five basic land types too — but they'd still have lost their original abilities to Blood Moon's layer-6 effect, gaining all five basic-type mana abilities instead.

Player count doesn't matter here: Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller, and Dryad of the Ilysian Grove affects only lands Addison controls, so in a multiplayer game other players' nonbasic lands are Mountains and their basic lands are unchanged.

question: Angelina has seven cards in their hand, controls [Trusted Advisor], and casts [Null Profusion]. After Angelina discards at the end of the turn, how many cards should they have in their hand?
answer:
Angelina should have two cards in hand.

Null Profusion sets Angelina's maximum hand size to two, and Trusted Advisor increases Angelina's maximum hand size by two. When multiple effects modify maximum hand size, they're applied in timestamp order (Trusted Advisor ruling #0, Null Profusion ruling #3). Here Trusted Advisor was already on the battlefield and Null Profusion entered afterward, so Trusted Advisor's +2 is applied first (7 + 2 = 9) and then Null Profusion's later effect overwrites it, simply setting the maximum to two. Had Null Profusion entered first and Trusted Advisor second, the maximum would instead be four.

At the beginning of Angelina's cleanup step, the turn-based action of discarding down to maximum hand size happens without using the stack, so Angelina discards until only two cards remain ([402.2], [514.1], [703.4n]). If Angelina still has seven cards at that point, that's five cards discarded.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Null Profusion resolved and is on the battlefield at the start of Angelina's cleanup step, and that Trusted Advisor's timestamp is earlier. If Null Profusion were somehow no longer on the battlefield at cleanup, only Trusted Advisor would apply and the maximum would be nine (so no discard from a seven-card hand). Note also that this discard only happens in the active player's own cleanup step — if it isn't Angelina's turn, they don't discard at all.

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; maximum hand size and the cleanup discard aren't player-count dependent.

answer_gold: Two. Trusted Advisor adds two to the maximum hand size (making it nine), and Null Profusion then sets the maximum hand to two.

question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
answer:
Nico's Thespian's Stage is now a land named Temple of Triumph with no land types and exactly one ability, "{T}: Add one mana of any color" — it has lost the Thespian's Stage copy ability, so Nico can't re-copy anything with it. Alayna's second Thespian's Stage, once its ability resolves, is an untapped-or-tapped-as-it-already-was land that's a full copy of Temple of Triumph ("This land enters tapped," "When this land enters, scry 1," "{T}: Add {R} or {W}") plus the Thespian's Stage copy ability, and Alpine Moon does not touch it.

Why:

Nico's Stage — the copy effect from Thespian's Stage is applied in layer 1 (CR 613.1a, 613.2a), so its copiable values are those of Temple of Triumph, except it also keeps "{2}, {T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability" (CR 707.9a, and Thespian's Stage ruling #0: the copy has no duration and it loses the {T}: Add {C} ability). Its name is therefore "Temple of Triumph," so Alpine Moon's chosen name matches. Alpine Moon affects lands opponents of Alayna control, and Nico is such an opponent. Its type-changing part applies in layer 4 (removing land types — Temple of Triumph has none, and per Alpine Moon ruling #1 the land card type and any supertypes stay) and its ability part in layer 6: lose all abilities, then gain "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Because "lose all abilities" is applied before the grant within the same effect, the granted mana ability survives, but the copied Temple abilities and the Stage's own copy ability are gone. Nico's land is still tapped or untapped exactly as it was — becoming a copy never untaps it (Thespian's Stage ruling #2).

Alayna's Stage — Alpine Moon only hits lands Alayna's opponents control, so her own land is unaffected. When she copies "Temple of Triumph," she copies its copiable values: Alpine Moon is a type-changing/ability-changing continuous effect, not a copy effect, so those changes are not copied (CR 707.2, Thespian's Stage ruling #3). This is true whether she targets a real Temple of Triumph or Nico's Stage — copying Nico's Stage yields Nico's copiable values (Temple of Triumph + the Stage copy ability, per CR 707.3/707.9a), stripped of Alpine Moon's effect. No enters-the-battlefield effects apply, so "enters tapped" and the scry 1 do nothing now (Thespian's Stage ruling #1); it just sits there with those abilities as text, plus "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" and the copy ability.

One wrinkle worth naming: Alayna's Stage is now also named "Temple of Triumph," but Alpine Moon only affects lands Alayna's *opponents* control, so it stays untouched. In a multiplayer game the same logic scales: every land named Temple of Triumph controlled by any opponent of Alayna gets stripped and gains the any-color mana ability; lands Alayna controls never do.

question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
answer:
Thraben Purebloods ends up as a green enchantment permanent named Thraben Purebloods with no abilities, no creature type, and no longer a creature.

How the two Auras combine (applied in timestamp order within each layer, rule 613.9, 613.5):

- Abilities: Kenrith's Transformation says the enchanted creature loses all abilities. Thraben Purebloods has none printed anyway, so nothing changes there. (If it later gained an ability it would keep it — Kenrith's Transformation ruling #6.)
- Card types (layer 4): Kenrith's Transformation makes Thraben Purebloods a green Elk creature; One with the Stars, applied later in timestamp order, makes it an enchantment and removes all other card types. Since One with the Stars has the later timestamp, it wins: Thraben Purebloods is an enchantment and is not a creature (613.9).
- Subtypes: losing the creature card type also strips the creature subtype Elk that Kenrith's Transformation granted (One with the Stars ruling #2; see also 205.1b on which types are retained). Any supertypes would be kept (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #3, One with the Stars ruling #2).
- Color: One with the Stars doesn't change color, so Kenrith's Transformation's color-setting effect still applies — Thraben Purebloods is green.
- Power/toughness: Kenrith's Transformation's base 3/3 still technically applies in layer 7b (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #2), but power and toughness are meaningless while Thraben Purebloods isn't a creature.

Order assumption: I'm assuming One with the Stars became attached after Kenrith's Transformation, as stated. If the timestamps were reversed (Kenrith's Transformation attached later), Kenrith's Transformation's "is a green Elk creature" would apply after One with the Stars and Thraben Purebloods would be a green Elk creature again (613.9).

One gap I can't close from the provided material: the rules given here don't include the state-based action for an Aura that's illegally attached, so I can't tell you from this context what happens to Kenrith's Transformation now that Thraben Purebloods is no longer a creature (its enchant ability is "enchant creature"; rule 702.5c only covers Auras with multiple enchant instances). One with the Stars itself remains legally attached, since it says "enchant creature or enchantment."

Nothing here depends on player count — the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Two effects are affecting the same creature: one from an Aura that says “Enchanted creature has flying” and one from an Aura that says “Enchanted creature loses flying.” Neither of these depends on the other, since nothing changes what they affect or what they’re doing to it. Applying them in timestamp order means the one that was generated last “wins.” The same process would be followed, and the same result reached, if either of the effects had a duration (such as “Target creature loses flying until end of turn”) or came from a non-Aura source (such as “All creatures lose flying”). answer_gold:
Thraben Purebloods becomes an enchantment with no abilities and with the color dictated by Kenrith's Transformation. When state-based actions are checked, Kenrith's Transformation is attached to an illegal target and is put into the graveyard. Thraben Purebloods then regains all characteristics except its type is only enchantment. State-based actions are checked again. Nothing happens, and Allen gets priority.

This is an interaction of continuous effects, so the layers will need to be considered. In this case, no changes occur until layer four. There are two effects occurring in this layer, so timestamps will need to be considered. Since Kenrith's Transformation was attached first, Thraben Purebloods maintains its status as a creature. Then, One with the Stars turns Thraben Purebloods into an enchantment and removes all other types. Thraben Purebloods is changed to the color dictated by Kenrith's Transformation in layer five. Thraben Purebloods loses all abilities in layer six due to Kenrith's Transformation. Lastly, Thraben Purebloods has its power and toughness set to the values stated in Kenrith's Transformation in layer seven. When state-based actions are checked, Kenrith's Transformation is attached to an enchantment and is put into the graveyard. State-based actions are checked again, and nothing happens.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
The result is a single face-down mutated permanent that is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types beyond creature, no mana cost, and no printed characteristics of its own — those come from the topmost component, the manifested card, which is face down (110.5, 702.140e, 730.2a). Underneath it is Trumpeting Gnarr.

Details:

1. Legality of the target: Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate ability requires a non-Human creature with the same owner (702.140a). A face-down manifested creature has no creature types at all, so it isn't a Human and is a legal target, assuming Avery owns it.

2. Merging: as the mutating creature spell Trumpeting Gnarr resolves with a legal target, it doesn't enter the battlefield separately; it merges with the manifested creature to form one object represented by both cards, and Avery chooses top or bottom (702.140c, 608.3d, 730.1, 730.2a). Avery puts the manifested card on top, so Trumpeting Gnarr is the bottom component.

3. Characteristics: a merged/mutated permanent has the characteristics of its topmost component (730.2a), and "its other characteristics are derived from the topmost card or token" (702.140e). Because the top component is face down, the permanent stays a 2/2 colorless nameless creature with no mana cost — Trumpeting Gnarr's name, 3/3 body, Beast type, and {1}{G}{U} mana cost do not apply. This is a copiable effect applied in layer 1a (613.2, 613.2a).

4. Abilities: a mutated permanent has all abilities of each card representing it (702.140e), so it does have Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities — mutate {3}{G/U}{G/U} and "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token" — even though it looks like a plain face-down 2/2. (Compare 707.3, where a face-down permanent that merely copies something keeps no abilities; here rule 702.140e specifically grants the abilities of every component.)

5. Trigger now: the merge is a mutate event, so the Trumpeting Gnarr trigger triggers and Avery creates one 3/3 green Beast creature token (702.140d).

6. Turning it face up: the top card is the manifested card, so the permanent can be turned face up for that card's mana cost if it's a creature card; doing so would make its characteristics those of that card (plus it would still keep the abilities of both components under 702.140e).

Assumption on ordering: I'm assuming Soul Summons fully resolved and the manifest was already on the battlefield before Trumpeting Gnarr was cast for its mutate cost, as stated. If Trumpeting Gnarr had instead been cast targeting some other creature, none of the above about the manifest would apply.

Player count makes no difference here — the interaction is entirely between Avery's own permanents, so it plays out identically in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. They cast another Spontaneous Flight targeting Mist Dragon. After that resolves they then use [Hex Parasite] to remove one flying counter. Does Mist Dragon have flying?
answer:
Yes — Mist Dragon has flying (and is 9/8 until end of turn).

Walking through the layer‑6 (ability adding/removing) effects in timestamp order (613.1, 613.1f, 613.7a):

1. First Spontaneous Flight resolves: a flying counter goes on Mist Dragon. Keyword counters are applied in layer 6, so Mist Dragon has flying. (Timestamp 1.)
2. April activates Mist Dragon's "{0}: This creature loses flying." That ability-removing effect has a later timestamp (2) and removes all instances of flying it sees (113.10b), so at that point Mist Dragon does not have flying. Note this effect lasts indefinitely — but it does not stop flying from being added later; there is no "can't have flying" effect here (113.11, 101.2a), and with adds and removes of the same ability the most recent one prevails (113.10c, 613.9).
3. Second Spontaneous Flight resolves: a second flying counter, timestamp 3, later than the lose‑flying effect. Applied last in layer 6, it gives Mist Dragon flying again.
4. Hex Parasite removes one flying counter. One flying counter still remains on Mist Dragon, so Mist Dragon still has flying, and the lose‑flying effect (timestamp 2) is still older than the remaining counter. Because the two flying counters are identical objects, it doesn't matter which one is removed — the surviving counter's grant is the most recent flying‑adding effect either way, so flying sticks. Hex Parasite also gives itself +1/+0 for the one counter removed; that pumps Hex Parasite, not Mist Dragon.

Power/toughness (layer 7c): base 4/4, +2/+2 from each Spontaneous Flight = 8/8 until end of turn. Hex Parasite's +1/+0 applies to Hex Parasite (making it 2/1 until end of turn), not to Mist Dragon.

If April wants to turn flying off again, she can simply activate "{0}: This creature loses flying" once more — a new activation gets a new, later timestamp and beats the remaining counter (613.9).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it's the same in a two‑player or multiplayer game, since only April's own permanents and effects are involved.

question: Avery casts [Vulpikeet] for its mutate cost, mutating under a 1/1 red Goblin creature token. They then cast [Rootborn Defenses], choosing to populate the merged permanent. What happens?
answer:
Populate works here, and the new token copies the merged permanent's characteristics including the abilities contributed by Vulpikeet.

Step by step:

1. Vulpikeet cast for its mutate cost {2}{W} is a mutating creature spell targeting a non-Human creature Avery owns; the 1/1 red Goblin token qualifies. As it resolves with a legal target it does not enter the battlefield — it merges with the Goblin token and the two become one object, a mutated permanent [702.140a, 702.140c, 608.3d, 730.1].
2. Avery chose to put Vulpikeet **under**, so the Goblin token is the topmost component. A mutated permanent has all abilities of each component, but its other characteristics come from the topmost component [702.140e]. So the permanent is a 1/1 red Goblin **token** with flying and "Whenever this creature mutates, put a +1/+1 counter on it," and Vulpikeet's own mutate trigger goes on the stack and puts a +1/+1 counter on it, making it 2/2 [702.140d, Vulpikeet].
3. Because the topmost component is a token, the merged permanent is a creature token Avery controls, so Rootborn Defenses' populate may choose it [701.36a, Rootborn Defenses].
4. Populate creates a token that's a copy of that creature token. Changes to an object's characteristics from merging with a permanent are copiable values applied in layer 1a [613.2a], so the new token is a 1/1 red Goblin with flying and the mutate-trigger ability. It is a single, ordinary token — not a mutated permanent, and it does not copy the +1/+1 counter (counters aren't copiable values), so it's 1/1.
5. Rootborn Defenses then gives indestructible until end of turn to creatures Avery controls at that moment, which includes both the merged permanent and the newly populated token [Rootborn Defenses ruling #0].

Note on the ordering choice: if Avery had instead put Vulpikeet **on top**, the topmost component would be a card, the permanent would not be a token, and populate could not choose it [702.140e, 701.36a].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players; both spells only involve Avery's own permanents. Simultaneous-choice rules (APNAP, [101.4]) would only matter if other players had to make choices at the same time.

question: Aimee controls [Fiend Artisan] and has four creature cards in their graveyard. Nico enchants it with [Mystic Subdual]. What is the power and toughness of Fiend Artisan?
answer:
Fiend Artisan is -1/1 (a power of -1 is treated as 0 for dealing damage, but the value itself is -1).

Why: Fiend Artisan's printed power and toughness are 1/1, and "This creature gets +1/+1 for each creature card in your graveyard" is a static ability of Fiend Artisan that would apply in layer 7c as a modification (CR 613.4c, 613.1g, 302.4c). It is not a characteristic-defining ability setting power/toughness (CR 604.3, 613.4a) — Fiend Artisan's box reads 1/1, not */*.

Mystic Subdual says "Enchanted creature gets -2/-0 and loses all abilities." The ability-removal part applies in layer 6, before layer 7. Because Fiend Artisan's +1/+1-per-creature-card ability is removed in layer 6, it never starts generating its layer 7c effect at all (CR 613.6 only preserves effects that had already begun applying in an earlier layer). So the +4/+4 from the four creature cards in Aimee's graveyard simply doesn't happen.

Then in layer 7c only Mystic Subdual's -2/-0 applies: 1/1 → -1/1.

Note the contrast with Mystic Subdual ruling #1: that ruling covers creatures whose power/toughness are printed as */* via a characteristic-defining ability, which become base 0/0 when they lose abilities and end up -2/0. Fiend Artisan is different because it has a fixed printed 1/1 plus a separate pump ability, so it lands at -1/1.

This doesn't depend on the player count — nothing here references opponents or the defending player, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games. Timing note: this is the state as long as Mystic Subdual remains attached; if Mystic Subdual leaves, Fiend Artisan's ability returns and it would be 5/5 with four creature cards in the graveyard.

question: Ari controls [Xathrid Gorgon]. Neriah controls a [Hexavus] and [Stonehewer Giant]. Ari activates Xathrid Gorgon to put a petrification counter on Stonehewer Giant which Neriah removes with Hexavus. Can Neriah activate Stonehewer Giant's activated ability?
answer:
No. Neriah still can't activate Stonehewer Giant's {1}{W}, {T} ability.

Xathrid Gorgon's ability creates a continuous effect that doesn't depend on the petrification counter staying on Stonehewer Giant. Per [Xathrid Gorgon ruling #0], if the counter is removed, the creature remains a colorless artifact with defender, and its activated abilities still can't be activated. The counter is just a marker; removing it with Hexavus's {1}, Remove a counter from another creature you control ability does not undo the effect.

Note that Neriah can legally use Hexavus this way (Hexavus's ability removes any kind of counter from another creature Neriah controls, and activating Hexavus is not activating Stonehewer Giant's ability). But the prohibition on Stonehewer Giant persists: a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5], and a "can't" effect takes precedence over permission [101.2a]. This holds regardless of table size — the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since the restriction is on Stonehewer Giant itself.

Timing note: I'm assuming the petrification counter was removed after Xathrid Gorgon's ability had already resolved. If Hexavus's ability were somehow used before Xathrid Gorgon's ability resolved, there would be no petrification counter yet to remove, and Xathrid Gorgon's ability would simply resolve and lock down Stonehewer Giant anyway (assuming Stonehewer Giant is still a legal target).

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Avalyn controls [Maritime Guard] and wants to cast [Glowstone Recluse] mutating onto the Maritime Guard and putting it on top. What will the resulting creature's P/T be?
answer:
The mutated creature will be 1/1 with no abilities.

Why: Mutate makes one permanent whose abilities are those of all cards involved, but whose other characteristics (including printed power/toughness) come from the topmost card or token — here Glowstone Recluse, so its copiable P/T is 2/3, not Maritime Guard's 1/3 [702.140e]. Then continuous effects are applied in layers [613.1, 302.4c].

- Layer 6: Humility makes all creatures lose all abilities, so the mutated permanent loses Reach and the mutate trigger.
- Layer 7b: Humility sets base power and toughness to 1/1 — an effect that sets P/T to a specific value/base value applies in this sublayer [613.4b, 208.4a, Base Power, Base Toughness]. Humility is the only P/T-setting effect here, so the result is 1/1. There are no 7c modifications [613.4c] and no switches [613.4d].

No +1/+1 counters: the "Whenever this creature mutates, put two +1/+1 counters on it" ability is already gone in layer 6 at the moment the mutation happens, since Humility was on the battlefield first, so nothing triggers. Had the trigger somehow existed and resolved, the two counters would be +1/+1 modifications applied in layer 7c on top of Humility's 1/1, making it 3/3 — counters are not removed by Humility [613.4c, 613.5].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Humility is on the battlefield before Glowstone Recluse's mutate spell resolves. If instead Humility entered the battlefield after the mutation (later timestamp), the mutate trigger would already have resolved and put two +1/+1 counters on; Humility would still set base P/T to 1/1 in layer 7b, and the counters would apply in 7c, making it 3/3 [613.4b, 613.4c, 613.7].

question: Alex controls [Magus of the Moon] and [Forgotten Monument]. Neil casts [Lizard, Connors's Curse] targeting Magus of the Moon. After Lizard, Connors's Curse has resolved, what are the characteristics of Forgotten Monument?
answer:
Forgotten Monument is still a nonbasic land named Forgotten Monument, but it is now "Land — Mountain" with no Cave subtype, and its only ability is the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}." It loses "{T}: Add {C}" and loses the ability granting other Caves "{T}, Pay 1 life: Add one mana of any color."

Why: Lizard, Connors's Curse's triggered ability makes Magus of the Moon lose all abilities (and become a green 4/4 Lizard) permanently — per the Lizard, Connors's Curse ruling, that effect doesn't end at end of turn. But that doesn't undo what Magus of the Moon does to lands. Under the layer system (CR 613.1), type-changing effects are applied in layer 4 (CR 613.1d) and ability-adding/removing effects in layer 6 (CR 613.1f), so Magus of the Moon's subtype-setting effect on nonbasic lands is applied before the effect that strips Magus of the Moon's abilities is considered — regardless of the order the effects started (Magus of the Moon ruling #0). So Forgotten Monument keeps being a Mountain.

As a Mountain it loses its other land types and printed abilities and gains "{T}: Add {R}" (Magus of the Moon ruling #4). Note {R} is red mana specifically; the colorless {C} it used to make is gone, and {C} is never interchangeable with generic or colored mana. Magus of the Moon doesn't touch names or supertypes (Magus of the Moon ruling #1), so Forgotten Monument is still named Forgotten Monument and is still nonbasic. Also, since Forgotten Monument is no longer a Cave, it wouldn't be picked up by another Cave-granting effect either.

Timeline assumption: I'm assuming Lizard, Connors's Curse's trigger has fully resolved and Magus of the Moon is still on the battlefield (now a 4/4 green Lizard with no abilities). If instead Magus of the Moon had left the battlefield, its continuous effect would end entirely and Forgotten Monument would revert to a Cave with its printed abilities. Player count doesn't matter here — the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since the effect applies to all nonbasic lands regardless of controller.

question: Ainsley enchants their [Colossus Hammer] with [Rune of Flight]. Then they equip it to [Skeletal Snake]. Does Skeletal Snake have flying?
answer:
Yes — Skeletal Snake has flying, and it's a 12/11.

Why: Rune of Flight is attached to Colossus Hammer, which is an Equipment, so Rune of Flight gives Colossus Hammer the ability "Equipped creature has flying." Per CR 613.7a, that granted ability's continuous effect uses Rune of Flight's timestamp, since that's later than Colossus Hammer's own timestamp. When Colossus Hammer becomes attached to Skeletal Snake, Colossus Hammer gets a new timestamp (CR 613.7e) and both of its abilities receive new timestamps, but their relative order is preserved (CR 613.7a) — Colossus Hammer's own "+10/+10 and loses flying" still comes first, and the Rune of Flight-granted "Equipped creature has flying" still comes second. This is exactly the example printed in CR 613.7a.

In layer 6 (ability-adding/removing), both effects apply in timestamp order: first Skeletal Snake loses flying, then it gains flying, so the later effect wins (CR 613.9, CR 113.10). In layer 7c, Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 makes the 2/1 Skeletal Snake a 12/11. Result: a 12/11 Skeletal Snake with flying.

Note that this is consistent with the Colossus Hammer rulings: Colossus Hammer only strips flying that's already there in an earlier-timestamped effect; a creature that gains flying afterward keeps it (Colossus Hammer ruling #2). Also, gaining flying only matters at all if something has flying to grant — here Rune of Flight supplies it even though Skeletal Snake had none printed (Colossus Hammer ruling #0).

Ordering assumption: I'm assuming Rune of Flight was attached to Colossus Hammer *before* Colossus Hammer was equipped, as stated. If instead you equipped Colossus Hammer first and then cast Rune of Flight on it, Rune of Flight's grant would simply have the later timestamp anyway and Skeletal Snake would still have flying. Player count doesn't change any of this; none of these effects depend on opponents or a defending player.

question: Ari controls [Magus of the Moon] enchanted with [Ichthyomorphosis]. Is Ari's [Dormant Volcano] a Mountain?

Yes. Ari's Dormant Volcano is a Mountain. Even though Ichthyomorphosis makes Magus of the Moon lose all its abilities, Magus of the Moon's type-changing effect on nonbasic lands still applies: effects that change subtypes are applied before effects that remove abilities, regardless of the order in which they started [Magus of the Moon ruling #0].

Details:
- Dormant Volcano is a nonbasic land (a Land with no basic land supertype), so it falls under Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains."
- As a result, Dormant Volcano loses its other land types and its own abilities ("This land enters tapped," the enters-the-battlefield sacrifice trigger, and "{T}: Add {C}{R}") and instead has the land type Mountain and the ability "{T}: Add {R}" [Magus of the Moon ruling #4], which matches the intrinsic ability every object with the Mountain basic land type has [305.6], [Mountain]. Note that's {R}, one red mana — not the {C}{R} Dormant Volcano would otherwise produce; {C} is colorless mana specifically, not generic.
- Magus of the Moon does not change names or supertypes, so Dormant Volcano is not literally a basic land and is not named "Mountain" [Magus of the Moon ruling #1].
- Magus of the Moon remains on the battlefield (Ichthyomorphosis makes it a blue Fish with base power and toughness 0/1), so its effect keeps applying.

This answer doesn't depend on player count — Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, so it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Averie controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
answer:
Wayward Angel ends up as a 6/6 black Creature — Angel Horror with no abilities.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1f/613.1g, 613.4a–c, 613.7):

- Layer 5 (color): Wayward Angel's threshold ability is active (7+ cards in Averie's graveyard) and its timestamp is earlier than Humility's, so Wayward Angel is black — and only black, not white and black (Wayward Angel ruling #0). Humility does nothing in this layer.
- Layer 6 (abilities): First the threshold ability grants trample and the upkeep sacrifice trigger (timestamp of Wayward Angel), then Humility, with the later timestamp, removes all abilities from all creatures. So Wayward Angel loses flying, vigilance, the threshold ability itself, trample, and the sacrifice trigger — it has no abilities at all.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): Humility sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1.
- Layer 7c (modifying P/T): Muraganda Petroglyphs checks the state as of this layer. Wayward Angel now truly has no abilities, so it gets +2/+2 → 3/3. Then the threshold ability's +3/+3 still applies: under CR 613.6, an effect that started applying in an earlier layer (here, the color change in layer 5) keeps applying in every later applicable layer even though the ability generating it was removed in layer 6 — exactly the principle spelled out in Humility ruling #2. That gives 6/6.

Note the interaction quirk: Muraganda Petroglyphs is not granting or removing anything, and "is black" is a characteristic-setting effect, not an ability (CR 113.12), so it never disqualifies Wayward Angel from the +2/+2.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Muraganda Petroglyphs and Wayward Angel were on the battlefield before Humility resolved, as stated. If Humility had the earliest timestamp instead, layer 7b would apply Humility's 1/1 first and then... actually with only these effects the 7b result is the same (Humility is the only 7b effect), so the answer would be unchanged; only a second base-setting effect (like Opalescence, per Humility ruling #0) would make timestamp order in 7b matter.

Player count doesn't change anything here — the rules applied are continuous-effect layering rules that work identically in two-player and multiplayer games; Humility affects all creatures regardless of controller.

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Urza's Saga becomes (say) a Mountain, loses its chapter abilities, and — per the card's own ruling — is immediately sacrificed as a state-based action. Nico keeps nothing from it except whatever abilities other effects had already granted it (which disappear with the permanent).

Why:

1. Jinx sets the land's subtype to a basic land type. Under rule [305.7], setting a land's subtype means the land loses its old land type (Urza's Saga) and loses all abilities generated from its rules text and old land types, gaining the basic type's mana ability instead. So the three chapter abilities (I, II, III) — which are keyword abilities printed in its text box, rule [107.15a] / [714.2b] — are gone.
2. Jinx changes only land subtypes. It doesn't change card types or supertypes ([305.7], [205.4b]), so the permanent is still an enchantment with the enchantment subtype Saga, and it still has its two lore counters.
3. [Urza's Saga ruling #1] directly covers this: if Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed. That ruling is authoritative for this interaction.
   Note the tension worth knowing: the current wording of the state-based action, rules [704.5s] and [714.4], only sacrifices "a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities" whose lore counters meet or exceed its final chapter number. Read strictly, a Saga with zero chapter abilities has no final chapter number and wouldn't be sacrificed. Follow the card ruling as given here; at a sanctioned event confirm with a judge which wording applies.
4. Abilities granted by other effects are not removed by [305.7]. So the "{T}: Add {C}" and the "{2}, {T}: Create a 0/0 Construct" abilities Urza's Saga gained from its own resolved chapter I and II triggers ([Urza's Saga ruling #5]) technically survive the type change — but only until the sacrifice, which happens immediately as a state-based action before anyone gets priority. If Nico had priority in response to Jinx, activating those abilities first is the way to get value; after Jinx resolves it's too late.

Chapter III never triggers, since no lore counter is added by Jinx and the Saga is gone before Nico's next precombat main phase turn-based action ([505.4], [703.4f], [714.3c]).

Player count doesn't matter here: this works identically at a two-player table and in multiplayer, since Jinx targets a single land and the sacrifice is performed by that permanent's controller, Nico.

question: Aaden activates [Inkmoth Nexus], equips [Colossus Hammer] to it, then activates Inkmoth Nexus again. What are the characteristics of Inkmoth Nexus?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus is an 11/11 colorless Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature land with flying and infect (plus its own two activated abilities).

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.7, timestamps: first activation = 1, Colossus Hammer attaching = 2, second activation = 3; per CR 613.7e Colossus Hammer got its timestamp when it became attached):

- Layer 4 (types): both activations of Inkmoth Nexus make it an artifact creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth — and it's still a land.
- Layer 5 (color): nothing changes it; Inkmoth Nexus stays colorless.
- Layer 6 (abilities): the first activation grants flying and infect (ts 1); Colossus Hammer's "loses flying" removes flying (ts 2); the second activation of Inkmoth Nexus re-grants flying and infect (ts 3). Since the latest effect in this layer adds flying back, Inkmoth Nexus has flying and infect.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): both activations set it to 1/1; the later one (ts 3) wins, so 1/1.
- Layer 7c (modifications): Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 applies on top, giving 11/11.

All of this lasts until end of turn for the animation effects; the +10/+10 and "loses flying" last as long as Colossus Hammer stays attached. question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: Alvin's Copy Artifact stops being a Dance of the Dead and becomes a 6/4 copy of Streetbreaker Wurm that keeps only the Mizzium Transreliquat ability "{1}{U}{R}: This artifact becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability." Because it never left the battlefield, its Dance of the Dead "when this Aura leaves the battlefield" trigger does not trigger, so the Viashino Warrior is NOT sacrificed 	it simply stays on the battlefield, no longer enchanted, no longer getting +1/+1 and no longer prevented from untapping.

Step by step:

1. Copy Artifact entering. Mizzium Transreliquat had used its second ability, which permanently makes it a copy of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the {1}{U}{R} ability (Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #0). Copy effects are part of copiable values, so Copy Artifact copying Mizzium Transreliquat copies that result (707.2, 707.3, Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3). Two replacement effects then apply as it enters, in the order Alvin chooses (616.1f): Copy Artifact's own effect first (giving it Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' copiable values, including "except it has Sakashima's other abilities" and the {1}{U}{R} ability, 707.9a/707.9b), then Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' copy ability.

2. Copying Dance of the Dead is legal because Mycosynth Lattice makes Dance of the Dead an artifact and March of the Machines then makes that noncreature artifact a creature (MV 2, so a 2/2) 	so it is "another creature you control." The resulting Copy Artifact is a Dance of the Dead with Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' other abilities, which includes the inherited {1}{U}{R} Mizzium Transreliquat ability (201.5b for the name-substitution in gained abilities).

3. Sacrificing March of the Machines to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked before state-based actions are checked matters a lot. While March of the Machines was out, the Copy Artifact/Dance of the Dead was itself a creature, and a creature Aura can't enchant anything (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3). Since March of the Machines is gone by the time state-based actions are next checked and by the time the trigger resolves, it is a normal (artifact) Aura again, so the trigger legally puts Viashino Warrior onto the battlefield tapped and attaches to it.

4. The activation. The Copy Artifact is still an artifact (Mycosynth Lattice), so it can activate {1}{U}{R}, and Streetbreaker Wurm is also an artifact thanks to Mycosynth Lattice, so it's a legal target. On resolution the Copy Artifact's copiable values are overwritten entirely by Streetbreaker Wurm's, except it keeps that {1}{U}{R} ability (707.2, 707.9a). It loses the Aura types and all Dance of the Dead text, and also loses Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' legend-rule and partner abilities.

5. No sacrifice trigger. Rule 707.4 states that a permanent copying a different object while remaining on the battlefield does not cause leaves-the-battlefield (or enters-the-battlefield) abilities to trigger. Dance of the Dead's "when this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" therefore never triggers, and it isn't even an ability of the permanent anymore. Viashino Warrior stays, and is now unattached (it can untap normally on Alvin's next untap step). Alvin's original Streetbreaker Wurm and its real Dance of the Dead are unaffected.

Timing caveat: I'm assuming March of the Machines was sacrificed before state-based actions were next checked and before the Dance of the Dead trigger resolved, as described. If instead state-based actions were checked while March of the Machines was still on the battlefield, the creature-Aura Copy Artifact would have been unattached and put into its owner's graveyard (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3), and then its leaves-the-battlefield ability would have made Alvin sacrifice the Viashino Warrior.

Player count: nothing here changes between two players and multiplayer, except that Eureka lets every player put permanents onto the battlefield; those choices are made in turn order starting with Alvin (101.4).

question: Ari casts [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze], with two spells having been cast before then. Nadia controls [Humility]. What will Ari's battlefield look like once the stack fully resolves and state-based actions are checked?
answer:
Ari ends up with three green Ooze creatures, all 1/1 with no abilities and no +1/+1 counters: two nontoken-... precisely, two Ooze tokens (not legendary) and the one nontoken Aeve, Progenitor Ooze (still legendary). Nothing dies to the legend rule.

Why:

1. Storm counts the two spells cast earlier this turn, so it creates two copies of Aeve, Progenitor Ooze as token spells. Per [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2], the two storm copies resolve and enter the battlefield one at a time, then the original Aeve, Progenitor Ooze resolves and enters ([608.1], [608.3a]).

2. Nadia's Humility reads "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." That applies in layer 6 (ability removal) and layer 7b (setting base P/T) ([613.1g], [613.5], [Humility ruling #2]).

3. Counters: the moment each Ooze is on the battlefield, Humility has already stripped its abilities, so the "Aeve enters with a +1/+1 counter on it for each other Ooze you control" ability isn't there to apply — no Ooze gets counters. (Even if any had, Humility's layer‑7b base‑setting is applied before layer‑7c counters, so they'd still only be 1/1 plus counters; here there are none.) Note that even if counters existed they wouldn't be copied by copy effects ([707.2]).

4. Legendary status: "Aeve isn't legendary if it's a token" is a supertype-changing effect that applies in layer 4, which is applied before Humility's layer‑6 ability removal — and per CR 613.6 an effect that starts applying keeps applying even though the generating ability is removed later in the process ([Humility ruling #2] shows the same pattern with Opalescence). I confirmed the layer walk: token = Creature — Ooze, no supertype, no abilities, 1/1; nontoken = Legendary Creature — Ooze, no abilities, 1/1. So only one legendary permanent named Aeve, Progenitor Ooze exists and the legend rule doesn't kill anything.

5. State-based actions are only checked after the whole spell/copy has finished resolving, not mid-resolution ([704.4]), and each 1/1 has toughness greater than 0, so all three survive.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Humility was already on the battlefield before Aeve, Progenitor Ooze resolved. If Nadia's Humility instead arrived after the Oozes entered, each Ooze would have entered with counters per [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2] (0, then 1, then 2), and after Humility they'd be 1/1 plus those counters — i.e., 1/1, 2/2, and 3/3.

Player count doesn't matter here: the provided rules that could vary with player count ([101.4] APNAP, [616.1f]) aren't engaged, so the result is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

question: Natalie controls [High Fae Trickster]. Allen activates the crew ability of [Capenna Express]. Before it resolves Natalie casts [One with the Stars] targeting Capenna Express. What happens when the crew ability resolves?
answer:
Natalie can't cast One with the Stars targeting Capenna Express at that moment — the crew ability is still on the stack, so Capenna Express is still just a noncreature artifact Vehicle and is not a legal target for an Aura that reads "Enchant creature or enchantment." The attempted cast is illegal and is rewound; Allen's crew ability then resolves normally and Capenna Express becomes an artifact creature (a 6/6) until end of turn.

Details:
- Crew is an activated ability: "Tap any number of other untapped creatures you control with total power N or greater: This permanent becomes an artifact creature until end of turn" [702.122a]. The creatures are tapped as a cost when Allen activates it; the type change happens only on resolution. Until then Capenna Express has no power or toughness and isn't a creature [208.3a].
- Because Capenna Express is neither a creature nor an enchantment while the crew ability is on the stack, it can't be chosen as the target of One with the Stars. Target legality is checked both on casting and again on resolution [608.2b].
- High Fae Trickster's "You may cast spells as though they had flash" lets Natalie cast One with the Stars at instant speed, but it doesn't change what the Aura can legally enchant.
- If instead Natalie waits until after the crew ability resolves, Capenna Express is then an artifact creature and is a legal target. One with the Stars would make it an enchantment that loses all other card types, and per One with the Stars ruling #1 it stays an enchantment even after the crew effect would have expired at end of turn.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Aitana casts [Finale of Devastation] with X = 10. Will the creature they find have haste?
answer:
Yes — the creature Aitana finds with Finale of Devastation will have haste, and it will be an 11/11.

Why: both effects apply in the layer system. Nico's Humility ("All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1") removes abilities in layer 6 and sets base P/T in layer 7b. Finale of Devastation, with X = 10, grants "+X/+X and haste until end of turn" — the haste grant also applies in layer 6, with a later timestamp than Humility (Humility was already on the battlefield when Finale of Devastation resolved). Within layer 6 effects apply in timestamp order, so Humility strips abilities first and then Finale of Devastation adds haste on top; nothing later takes it away. Humility does not continuously re-strip abilities granted after it.

Power/toughness: layer 7b Humility sets base 1/1, then layer 7c Finale of Devastation's +10/+10 applies, giving 11/11.

The found creature is affected: Finale of Devastation's pump/haste applies to creatures you control as the spell finishes resolving, and the creature just put onto the battlefield does get +X/+X and haste (Finale of Devastation ruling #2); no player can act in between (Finale of Devastation ruling #0).

What haste does: it lets the creature attack, and lets Aitana activate its abilities with {T} or untap symbols in the cost, even though it hasn't been under Aitana's control continuously since her turn began — i.e., it ignores the "summoning sickness" rule (302.6, 702.10a–c). Note that Humility still strips any other abilities the creature had, so it can attack as a vanilla 11/11 with haste and nothing else.

Assumption on timing: Humility was on the battlefield before Finale of Devastation resolved (as stated). If instead Humility somehow entered the battlefield after the haste was granted, Humility's later timestamp in layer 6 would remove that haste and the creature would be 1/1 plus the +10/+10 from layer 7c, i.e. 11/11 without haste.

Player count doesn't matter here — the provided rules on haste, summoning sickness, and layers work identically at a two-player or multiplayer table.

question: Avery's [Unlicensed Hearse] has exiled five cards, and they activate its crew ability. After that resolves, Avery casts [Dress Down]. What does Unlicensed Hearse look like?
answer:
Unlicensed Hearse becomes a 0/0 colorless Artifact Creature — Vehicle with no abilities, and it's put into Avery's graveyard as a state-based action (unless something else is boosting its toughness).

Why, step by step through the layer system:

- Layer 4 (types): Crew 2 made Unlicensed Hearse an artifact creature until end of turn ("This permanent becomes an artifact creature until end of turn," per rule 702.122a). Dress Down does not remove that — it only removes abilities — so Unlicensed Hearse stays an artifact creature with the Vehicle subtype.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Dress Down says "Creatures lose all abilities." Unlicensed Hearse is a creature at this point, so it loses its {T} exile ability, its Crew 2 ability, and — importantly — its characteristic-defining ability "Unlicensed Hearse's power and toughness are each equal to the number of cards exiled with it."
- Layer 7a (CDA power/toughness): that CDA no longer exists to apply, so nothing sets Unlicensed Hearse's power and toughness. A creature with no P/T-setting effect is 0/0, and a creature with 0 toughness is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. The five exiled cards no longer matter, because the ability that counted them is gone.

Note the ordering matters and it's the one you described: crewing resolved first, then Dress Down entered. Dress Down affects creatures as they exist while it's on the battlefield, and Unlicensed Hearse was already a creature, so it's caught. (Compare Dress Down ruling #0: Dress Down doesn't strip abilities granted after it entered — but here the CDA was already on the card, so it is stripped.) If instead Avery cast Dress Down first and then tried to crew, Unlicensed Hearse would have lost Crew 2 while it's... actually it isn't a creature yet at that point, so Dress Down wouldn't touch it, and crewing would then turn a still-CDA-having Vehicle into a 5/5 creature — the reverse order is much better for Avery. Also compare Unlicensed Hearse ruling #0, the same 0/0 death happens when you crew before exiling anything.

Player count doesn't change any of this; the provided rules on crew, layers, and state-based actions are the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question:
Alison controls [Mycosynth Lattice], an [Animate Dead] attached to a [Great-Horn Krushok] that it returned to the battlefield, a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that copied [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] with its second ability, and a [Southern Elephant] enchanted by a [Deep Freeze].

Alison casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield. Alison then puts [Sculpting Steel] onto the battlefield, choosing to copy the Mizzium Transreliquat and then choosing to copy the Animate Dead with its new copy ability. They choose to enchant a [Gigantosaurus] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines.

After Sculpting Steel's trigger resolves and returns the Gigantosaurus to the battlefield, Alison activates the ability of the Sculpting Steel to turn it into a copy of Deep Freeze. After that resolves, they casts [Enchantment Alteration] to attach it to the Southern Elephant. What happens?
answer:
Bottom line: the Sculpting Steel ends up in Alison's graveyard, and Gigantosaurus goes back to being a 10/10 with its abilities. Southern Elephant is unaffected (it keeps its original Deep Freeze).

Step by step:

1. **Sculpting Steel's entry.** Copying Mizzium Transreliquat copies the Transreliquat's *current* copiable values, which are Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the Transreliquat's own "{1}{U}{R}: This artifact becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability" (707.9a, 613.1a, Sculpting Steel ruling #4, Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3). So Sculpting Steel enters with Sakashima of a Thousand Faces's replacement ability and applies it, entering as a copy of Animate Dead "except it has Sakashima's other abilities" — which on this object include the {1}{U}{R} copy ability (201.5b, 707.9a, Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #0/#9). Animate Dead is a legal choice only because Mycosynth Lattice makes it an artifact and March of the Machines makes noncreature artifacts creatures; no state-based actions are checked during Eureka's resolution, so nothing has fallen off yet.

2. **March of the Machines is sacrificed to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked** before Eureka finishes, so when SBAs are finally checked the Auras aren't creatures and nothing is unattached (compare Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3, which is what *would* have killed the Auras had SBAs been checked while March of the Machines was out).

3. **The trigger resolves:** Sculpting Steel loses "enchant creature card in a graveyard," gains "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," returns Gigantosaurus to the battlefield, and attaches to it (9/10 from Animate Dead's -1/-0).

4. **Activating {1}{U}{R} to copy Deep Freeze.** Deep Freeze is an artifact thanks to Mycosynth Lattice, so it's a legal target. Sculpting Steel's copiable values become Deep Freeze plus that ability; the Animate Dead text (the -1/-0, the leave-the-battlefield sacrifice trigger, and "enchant creature card in a graveyard") is gone. But the ability *granted* by the resolved trigger, "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," is a non-copy continuous effect and survives the copy change (707.4). Attached to Gigantosaurus, both "enchant creature" and that granted restriction are satisfied, so it stays on; Gigantosaurus becomes a 0/4 blue Wall with defender and no other abilities (Deep Freeze ruling #2).

5. **Enchantment Alteration.** Sculpting Steel is an Aura attached to a creature, and Southern Elephant is another creature, so the spell resolves and attaches it (new timestamp, 701.3c). But Southern Elephant was *not* put onto the battlefield with this Aura, so the granted enchant restriction is violated — the Aura is attached illegally and is put into Alison's graveyard the next time state-based actions are checked. Gigantosaurus is *not* sacrificed, because the Animate Dead leave-the-battlefield trigger was overwritten by the Deep Freeze copy effect. Gigantosaurus, no longer enchanted, is a normal 10/10.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked's sacrifice of March of the Machines happens during Eureka's resolution, as stated. If March of the Machines had somehow stayed on the battlefield past a state-based action check, every Aura (including both Animate Deads) would have been an artifact creature, would have become unattached, and would have gone to the graveyard immediately (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3).

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, Eureka's "starting with you, each player may put a permanent card" gives the other players chances to act in turn order (101.4), but that doesn't change any of the above for Alison's permanents.

question: Alex controls [Karametra, God of Harvests], and then casts [Opalescence]. Their devotion to white is 2. Is Karametra, God of Harvests a creature? If so, what is its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — Karametra, God of Harvests is a creature, and it's a 5/5 (a Legendary Enchantment Creature with no creature subtype).

Why: devotion to green and white counts mana symbols that are green, white, or both among permanents Alex controls (700.5a). Karametra, God of Harvests contributes {G}{W} = 2 and Opalescence contributes {W}{W} = 2, so devotion to green and white is 4 — less than seven. So Karametra's own ability applies.

Layer 4 (types), in timestamp order (613.1, 613.7):
- Karametra, God of Harvests (earlier timestamp) removes the creature type and the God subtype from itself; it stays a Legendary Enchantment [Karametra, God of Harvests ruling #15].
- Opalescence (later timestamp) then applies to "each other non-Aura enchantment" — Karametra, God of Harvests qualifies — and makes it a creature in addition to its other types. Because Opalescence's timestamp is later, the net result in layer 4 is that Karametra, God of Harvests IS a creature. It does not regain the God subtype.

question: Autumn animates [Inkmoth Nexus] and attacks with it. Nayeli then flashes in [Dress Down]. What does Inkmoth Nexus look like?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus is a 1/1 colorless Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature land with no abilities at all, and it's still attacking.

How the layers get there (CR 613.1, applied in order):
- Layer 4 (types): Autumn's activated ability makes Inkmoth Nexus an artifact creature Phyrexian Blinkmoth, still a land.
- Layer 6 (abilities): the animation ability first grants flying and infect; then Nayeli's Dress Down, with a later timestamp, says "Creatures lose all abilities" — since Inkmoth Nexus is a creature at this point, it loses everything: flying, infect, its "{T}: Add {C}" mana ability, and even the "{1}: This land becomes a 1/1..." activated ability itself.
- Layer 7b (power/toughness): the animation effect still sets Inkmoth Nexus to 1/1. Losing the ability in layer 6 does not undo this — CR 613.6 says an effect that has started to apply keeps applying in every other applicable layer even if the ability generating it is removed during the process.

Practical consequences: Inkmoth Nexus is still an attacking creature, but with no flying it can be blocked by anything, and with no infect its combat damage is normal damage to the defending player rather than poison counters. It also can't be tapped for {C} while Dress Down is out (that mana ability is gone), and Autumn can't re-activate the {1} animation ability from Inkmoth Nexus while it's a creature with no abilities. Dress Down sacrifices itself at the beginning of the end step, after which Inkmoth Nexus regains its printed abilities; the animation effect, if it's still that turn, keeps it a 1/1 artifact creature land but the flying/infect grant is gone for good, since layer 6 has already been resolved with Dress Down's later timestamp — recheck the board state at that time rather than assuming flying and infect come back.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Dress Down entered after Inkmoth Nexus was already animated and attacking (as stated). If Dress Down were already on the battlefield first and Autumn then activated the animation, the animation would have the later timestamp and Inkmoth Nexus would keep flying and infect until Dress Down's continuous effect is re-checked — but Dress Down's effect is continuous and applies to creatures continuously, so it would still strip them; the difference is only in ordering within layer 6, which the given rules resolve by timestamp.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table (Autumn simply chose a defending player when attacking).

question: Aaron equips [Skullclamp] onto [Champion of the Flame]. Does Champion of the Flame die?
answer:
No. Champion of the Flame survives, and Skullclamp's draw-two trigger does not happen.

Math: Champion of the Flame is base 1/1. Its own ability gives it +2/+2 for each Aura and Equipment attached to it, and Skullclamp is an Equipment attached to it, so that's +2/+2. Skullclamp itself grants the equipped creature +1/-1. Total: 1/1 +2/+2 +1/-1 = 4/2. Since its toughness is 2, not 0 or less, the state-based action that puts a creature with toughness 0 or less into its owner's graveyard never applies [704.5f], and state-based actions are checked automatically without using the stack [704.1]. Because Champion of the Flame doesn't die (i.e., isn't put into a graveyard from the battlefield) [700.4], Skullclamp's "Whenever equipped creature dies, draw two cards" ability never triggers.

Two caveats:
- If Champion of the Flame already has 2 or more damage marked on it this turn, that damage is now lethal against its new toughness of 2 and it will be destroyed as a state-based action; Skullclamp would then trigger. I'm assuming no damage is marked. The reverse case is also worth knowing: if you later move Skullclamp to another creature, Champion of the Flame loses the +2/+2 as well as the -1, and previously nonlethal damage can become lethal [Champion of the Flame ruling #0].
- Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

If an effect then turns the creature white (layer 5), it gets +1/+1 from Honor of the Pure (layer 7c), becoming 3/3. If the creature’s color is later changed to red (layer 5), Honor of the Pure’s effect stops applying to it, and it will return to being 2/2. Gray Ogre, a 2/2 creature, is on the battlefield. An effect puts a +1/+1 counter on it (layer 7c), making it 3/3. A spell targeting it that says “Target creature gets +4/+4 until end of turn” resolves (layer 7c), making it 7/7. An enchantment that says “Creatures you control get +0/+2” enters the battlefield (layer 7c), making it 7/9. An effect that says “Target creature becomes 0/1 until end of turn” is applied to it (layer 7b), making it 5/8 (0/1, with +4/+4 from the resolved spell, +0/+2 from the enchantment, and +1/+1 from the counter).

question: In their first main phase, Alexandra activates [Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance] to create two tokens, and Nehemiah responds with [Dress Down]. What happens with the tokens?
answer:
The two tokens are still created, and they still have haste. Dress Down doesn't stop token creation at all.

Details:

1. Dress Down resolves first (it was cast in response, so it's on top of the stack), setting up its continuous effect "Creatures lose all abilities." Then Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance's channel ability resolves and creates two 1/1 colorless Spirit creature tokens on the battlefield [701.7a]. A token fails to be created only if a rule or effect says a permanent with one of its characteristics can't enter the battlefield [111.5]; Dress Down says nothing of the kind, so both tokens are created normally.

2. The 1/1 Spirit tokens have no printed abilities, so Dress Down's ability-stripping effect has nothing to remove from them.

3. The haste sticks. Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance grants haste as part of the same resolution, which is an ability granted after Dress Down was already on the battlefield; per Dress Down ruling #0, an ability granted to a creature after Dress Down has entered is not lost. So Alexandra can attack with the two Spirits this turn.

4. Note on Dress Down's own text: it also draws Nehemiah a card on entry and is sacrificed at the beginning of the end step, so the ability-loss effect goes away then (unless Dress Down itself became a creature and thus lost that sacrifice trigger, per Dress Down ruling #1).

Timing assumption: I assumed Nehemiah's Dress Down resolves before the Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance ability, which is what "responds" means. If instead Dress Down somehow resolved before the channel ability was activated, the result is identical — the tokens are created and keep the haste granted to them at that time.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Aubree casts [Blood Moon]. Nikolas activates [Inkmoth Nexus]'s ability in response. What will Inkmoth Nexus look like after everything resolves? What will it look like next turn?
answer:
After everything resolves, Inkmoth Nexus is a 1/1 land artifact creature with the land type Mountain and exactly one ability: "{T}: Add {R}." It has no flying, no infect, no {T}: Add {C}, and no Phyrexian Blinkmoth land-type text — but it is still a 1/1 creature.

Why (CR 613.6 layer order; Inkmoth Nexus's ability resolved first, so it has the earlier timestamp, and Blood Moon's static effect starts applying when Blood Moon resolves, later):
- Layer 4 (type-changing, CR 613.1d): Inkmoth Nexus's ability makes it an artifact creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth that's still a land. Then Blood Moon applies, changing its land subtype to Mountain (Blood Moon ruling #2). Blood Moon only changes land types and doesn't touch supertypes or the name (Blood Moon ruling #1), so Inkmoth Nexus remains a land artifact creature, just with Mountain in place of its other land types.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Inkmoth Nexus's ability grants flying and infect first; then Blood Moon, with the later timestamp, strips all of the land's abilities and grants "{T}: Add {R}" (Blood Moon ruling #2). Because Blood Moon applies after, the granted flying and infect are removed too, and the {T}: Add {C} and the {1} animation ability are gone.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): the "becomes a 1/1" part of Inkmoth Nexus's ability still applies. Per CR 613.6, once an effect starts applying in one layer it keeps applying in every other applicable layer even though the ability generating it has been removed — so Inkmoth Nexus is 1/1 despite no longer having the ability that animated it.

Next turn: Inkmoth Nexus's animation was "until end of turn," so it wears off in the cleanup step. With Blood Moon still on the battlefield, next turn Inkmoth Nexus is simply a nonbasic land — Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}" and nothing else. Nikolas can no longer activate the {1} animation ability, because Blood Moon has removed it.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nikolas activated in response, so Inkmoth Nexus's ability resolved before Blood Moon. If instead Blood Moon had already resolved first, Nikolas couldn't activate the ability at all — Blood Moon would already have removed it.

Player count doesn't matter here; the provided rules on layers apply identically in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Niko controls [Urza's Saga] on chapter 2. Ainsley casts [Magus of the Moon]. What happens to Urza's Saga?
answer:
Urza's Saga is put into Niko's graveyard immediately — Niko sacrifices it as a state-based action.

Why: Magus of the Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." That makes Urza's Saga a Mountain, which sets its land subtype to Mountain and removes its rules text (leaving "{T}: Add {R}"), so it loses its chapter I, II, and III abilities. It does not, however, lose the enchantment subtype Saga (Magus of the Moon changes land types only, and per [Magus of the Moon ruling #1] it doesn't touch names or supertypes either).

So Urza's Saga is still a Saga permanent, but it now has no chapter abilities. Rule [704.5s]/[714.4] only sacrifices a Saga that has one or more chapter abilities and enough lore counters — but [Urza's Saga ruling #1] states this case explicitly: "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed." Timing note: Magus of the Moon must resolve first. While Ainsley's Magus of the Moon is still on the stack, Urza's Saga is unaffected — Niko can still activate its chapter II Construct-making ability (and hold priority to do so) before Magus of the Moon resolves. Any Construct token already created stays; only Urza's Saga itself is sacrificed. Niko also loses the chapter III search, since chapter III will never trigger.

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: Magus of the Moon affects every nonbasic land in play, so every player's Urza's Saga (and any similar Saga land) is sacrificed by its own controller.

question: Nico controls [Dress Down], and Aya activates [Inkmoth Nexus]. What does it look like?
answer:
Aya's Inkmoth Nexus becomes a 1/1 colorless Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature land with flying and infect — it keeps flying and infect despite Nico's Dress Down, but loses its own "{T}: Add {C}" and "{1}: This land becomes..." abilities.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613):
- Layer 4 (types): Inkmoth Nexus's activated ability makes it an artifact creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth — that's still a land.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Two effects apply here, in timestamp order. Dress Down ("Creatures lose all abilities") has the earlier timestamp — it was already on the battlefield — and Inkmoth Nexus is a creature by layer 4, so Dress Down strips everything, including the mana ability and the animation ability itself. Then the animation effect, with the later timestamp, adds flying and infect back. Under CR 613.6, that effect started applying in layer 4, so it continues to apply in layers 6 and 7 even though Dress Down removed the ability that generated it.
- Layer 7b: the animation sets power/toughness to 1/1.

Order assumption: I'm assuming Dress Down was already on the battlefield when Aya activated Inkmoth Nexus. If instead Nico casts Dress Down (it has flash) after the ability resolves, Dress Down has the later timestamp and applies second in layer 6 — then Inkmoth Nexus would be a 1/1 artifact creature land with no abilities at all (no flying, no infect), still 1/1 since that's layer 7.

Since infect is stripped only in that second ordering, note the combat consequence: in the assumed ordering, Inkmoth Nexus still deals damage to creatures as -1/-1 counters and to players as poison counters. This analysis doesn't depend on player count — Dress Down affects all creatures regardless of controller, so it works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

question: Ariana controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue." Nico casts [Dress Down]. What color are Painter's Servant and Dress Down?
answer:
Both Painter's Servant and Dress Down are blue (mono-blue).

Painter's Servant: it is printed with mana cost {2}, so it is normally colorless (rule 202.2a). Painter's Servant's own static ability makes all permanents the chosen color, blue, in addition to their other colors, and it applies to Painter's Servant itself. Color-changing effects are applied in layer 5, while Dress Down's "Creatures lose all abilities" is an ability-removing effect applied in layer 6 (rule 613.1e). Because layer 5 is applied before layer 6, Painter's Servant's ability is still present and its color effect is applied to everything in layer 5; per CR 613.6 that effect keeps applying even though the generating ability is stripped in layer 6. So once Dress Down has resolved, Painter's Servant is a blue 1/3 Artifact Creature — Scarecrow with no abilities. Since it was colorless, it just becomes blue, not "blue and colorless" (Painter's Servant ruling #0).

Dress Down: its mana cost is {1}{U}, so it is already blue (rule 202.2a), and Painter's Servant only adds blue "in addition" (Painter's Servant ruling #5), which changes nothing. Dress Down is blue. Note also that Dress Down is an enchantment, not a creature, so it never loses its own abilities to itself.

Assumption on timing: I'm answering for the state after Dress Down has resolved and is on the battlefield. While Dress Down is still on the stack, Painter's Servant obviously still has all its abilities and is likewise blue, so the color answer is the same either way.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players; Painter's Servant affects all cards, spells, and permanents regardless of controller.

question: Anabella controls [Blood Moon] and enchants their [Sunlit Marsh] with [Urban Utopia]. What colors can it tap for?
answer:
Sunlit Marsh can tap for any one color: {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} (one mana of your choice each time you tap it). It loses its {W}/{B} abilities and does NOT keep a Mountain's {R} ability.

Why: I'm assuming Blood Moon was already on the battlefield when Urban Utopia became attached (the order given in the question). Working through the layer system:

- Layer 4 (types): Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Sunlit Marsh is nonbasic, so it loses the Plains and Swamp subtypes and is just a Mountain [Blood Moon ruling #1, Blood Moon ruling #2].
- Layer 6 (abilities), timestamp 1 — Blood Moon: it strips all of Sunlit Marsh's other abilities and gives it "{T}: Add {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #2], which is the intrinsic Mountain ability [305.6, Mountain].
- Layer 6, timestamp 2 — Urban Utopia: enchanted land has "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Because Urban Utopia's ability-granting effect has the later timestamp, it applies after Blood Moon's ability-removal, so the granted ability sticks. Urban Utopia doesn't remove other abilities and doesn't change land types [Urban Utopia ruling #0] — but Blood Moon's earlier removal already wiped the {T}: Add {R} that the Mountain type produced, and the type-based ability isn't re-granted after the removal in this ordering.

So the end state is: Land — Mountain, with exactly "{T}: Add one mana of any color." The five colors are white, blue, black, red, green [105.1], so tapping it produces any one of {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, {G} — you choose on resolution of the mana ability [605.1]. Note this is a real color, never colorless {C}.

If instead Urban Utopia had been attached first and Blood Moon entered afterward, Blood Moon's later-timestamped ability removal would strip the granted "any color" ability too, and Sunlit Marsh would tap only for {R}.

Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Avery enchants their [Hall] with [Unbridled Growth]. Next turn, Nickolas casts [Blood Moon]. What colors of mana can Hall tap for?
answer:
Hall can tap for any one color of mana — white, blue, black, red, or green (one mana per tap). Blood Moon does not turn off Unbridled Growth's granted ability.

Why:

1. Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Hall is a nonbasic land, so this type-changing effect applies in the type-changing layer: Hall's subtypes become just Mountain, and per the Blood Moon ruling it loses its other land types and its own printed abilities — so Hall's printed "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" and "{4}, {T}: Investigate" are gone, and it instead has the intrinsic Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}" [305.6, Blood Moon ruling #2].
2. Unbridled Growth grants the enchanted land "{T}: Add one mana of any color." That's an ability-adding effect applied in the ability layer, which comes after the type-changing layer. Blood Moon's ability loss is a consequence of the type change in the earlier layer; it does not strip abilities granted later in the ability layer. So Unbridled Growth's ability survives and is still on Hall.

Running the layer resolution confirms Hall ends up as a Land — Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}" (intrinsic from the Mountain subtype) and "{T}: Add one mana of any color" (from Unbridled Growth). Since Hall has only one {T} to give, you tap it once and choose any of the five colors [105.1, 106.1a]. Note Hall can no longer Investigate, and its "enters tapped" ability is gone too (irrelevant while it's already on the battlefield).

Timing note: I'm assuming Unbridled Growth was already attached before Blood Moon resolved, as stated. The order doesn't matter here — layers are applied by layer first, not by which resolved first, so even if Blood Moon had come first and Unbridled Growth were attached afterward, Hall would still tap for any color.

Player count doesn't change anything: Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: What layer does [Grand Abolisher]'s "During your turn, your opponents can't cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures, or enchantments." ability apply in?
answer:
Grand Abolisher's ability doesn't apply in any layer. The layer system (rule 613.1) exists only to determine the values of an object's characteristics — copiable values (layer 1), control (layer 2), abilities (layer 6), and so on. Grand Abolisher's ability doesn't change any object's characteristics; it's a static ability generating a continuous effect that says something can't happen (your opponents can't cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures, or enchantments during your turn). Such "can't happen" effects aren't replacement effects and aren't characteristic-modifying effects; they simply prohibit the action, and a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated (rules 614.17 and 602.5).

So there's no timestamp/dependency ordering question (rules 613.3, 613.7, 613.8) for it — it just applies whenever a player would try to cast or activate during your turn. In a multiplayer game the ability works the same way, applying to every opponent at the table during your turn, not just one.

Two scope notes from the card's rulings: Grand Abolisher doesn't stop opponents from activating abilities of artifact, creature, or enchantment cards in zones other than the battlefield, such as cycling from hand (Grand Abolisher ruling #1), and it doesn't affect triggered or static abilities (Grand Abolisher ruling #0).
